Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • “great frogs with jewels in their foreheads”: An old belief held that the toad carried a precious stone, the toadstone, in its head, a cure for poison. Shakespeare used it in As You Like It: “Sweet are the uses of adversity, / Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous, / Wears yet a precious jewel in his head.”
  • “such as a dusty sparrow falling”: Jesus says of the sparrows, “one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29), and Hamlet answers his friend’s fears with “There is special providence in the fall of a sparrow.” Catherine later counts “falling sparrows, falling leaves, drops of water, grains of sand.”
  • “If ears could see, if eyes could hear”: Bottom wakes from his enchanted night in A Midsummer Night’s Dream with the senses mixed up: “The eye of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man’s hand is not able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was.” Bottom is parodying 1 Corinthians 2:9.

Chapter 3

  • “She dismissed the insubstantial fabric of the dream”: The phrase echoes Prospero in Shakespeare’s The Tempest: “And, like the baseless fabric of this vision, . . . this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff / As dreams are made on.”
  • “those who died but once, those who could not afford to die twice”: Julius Caesar says in Shakespeare’s play, “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.”
  • “our good works should not live after us”: Miss MacIntosh reverses Mark Antony in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: “The evil that men do lives after them; / The good is oft interred with their bones.”

Chapter 5

  • “seeing the breath on the mirror where there was no breath, the feather move where there was no feather”: Holding a mirror or a feather to the lips was the old test for death. King Lear, holding the dead Cordelia, calls, “Lend me a looking-glass; / If that her breath will mist or stain the stone, / Why, then she lives,” and then, “This feather stirs; she lives!”
  • “this womb of time”: Iago says, “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Othello 1.3).
  • “in his second childhood”: In Shakespeare’s As You Like It, Jaques’s seven ages of man end in “second childishness and mere oblivion.”

Chapter 6

  • “To thine own self be true, and it will follow as the day the night”: Polonius gives this advice to his son Laertes in Hamlet (1.3): “This above all: to thine own self be true, / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man.” Homer gets it backwards, “as the day the night.”
  • “come to the wedding feast and had stayed for the funeral”: Hamlet reversed: “the funeral baked meats / Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables” (Hamlet 1.2).
  • “it had not been a marriage of true souls”: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 116: “Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments. Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds.” Later Madge asks whether love can “alter.”
  • “Oh, Romeo, oh, Romeo!”: Juliet’s “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2).
  • “love is blind”: “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see” (The Merchant of Venice 2.6).
  • “Ding, dong, bell”: Ariel’s song for a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies . . . Ding-dong, bell.” Madge’s father drowned. The nursery rhyme “Ding, dong, bell, / Pussy’s in the well” also ends in drowning.
  • “She was Juliet, and I was Romeo”: In the play Romeo kisses Juliet, believing her dead, and drinks poison before she wakes from the sleeping potion.

Chapter 7

  • “A fool, Lear in the storm”: In Shakespeare’s King Lear, the “storm” is both a physical and metaphorical force. Lear is exposed to a violent natural storm on the heath, symbolizing his internal turmoil and the chaos of his kingdom after he disowns his loyal supporters and his loving daughter Cordelia. This exposure forces him to confront his own mortality and the suffering of others, leading to a shift in his perspective and, ultimately, a descent into madness. It is a metaphorical description that situates old Doc in the tradition of tragic figures overwhelmed by chaos, emphasizing themes of madness, vulnerability, and existential struggle that run through the novel.
  • “I know old Gertrude from away back”: Gertrude may be named after the character in Hamlet by Shakespeare. Both Gertrudes embody the tragic consequences of familial and marital complexities: Miss MacIntosh’s Gertrude through literal murder and madness, Shakespeare’s Gertrude through moral ambiguity and political betrayal. They both represent the fragility of women’s positions within patriarchal and violent family systems, caught between roles as wives, mothers, and individuals subjected to forces beyond their control. Their characters explore themes of guilt, innocence, and the ambiguity of human motives, complicating simplistic moral judgments. Both have a presence associated with death and decay, whether physical or psychological, underscoring the novel’s and play’s meditation on mortality.
  • “no lock which could not be opened at last by the locksmith”: The proverb “Love laughs at locksmiths” comes from Shakespeare’s Venus and Adonis.
  • “the drunken sexton who used to dance a merry jig when anybody died”: Hamlet’s gravedigger sings at his work: “Has this fellow no feeling of his business, that he sings at grave-making?” (Hamlet 5.1).
  • “It was that skull the children played with”: “Alas, poor Yorick!” Hamlet holds the jester’s skull (Hamlet 5.1).
  • “She was Mrs. Hathaway, and she became Mrs. Hathaway”: Shakespeare’s wife was Anne Hathaway, a fitting married name for a Gertrude straight out of Hamlet.

Chapter 7

  • “I know old Gertrude from away back”: Gertrude may be named after the character in Hamlet by Shakespeare. Both Gertrudes embody the tragic consequences of familial and marital complexities: Miss MacIntosh’s Gertrude through literal murder and madness, Shakespeare’s Gertrude through moral ambiguity and political betrayal. They both represent the fragility of women’s positions within patriarchal and violent family systems, caught between roles as wives, mothers, and individuals subjected to forces beyond their control. Their characters explore themes of guilt, innocence, and the ambiguity of human motives, complicating simplistic moral judgments. Both have a presence associated with death and decay, whether physical or psychological, underscoring the novel’s and play’s meditation on mortality.

Chapter 7

  • “What did he expect, marrying his brother’s wife”: Levirate marriage is the custom where the brother of a deceased man is obliged to marry his brother’s widow. Deuteronomy 25:5 commands it, and Leviticus 20:21 forbids it. Henry VIII used Leviticus to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, his brother’s widow. In Shakespeare’s Hamlet, Gertrude, Hamlet’s mother, marries her husband’s brother Claudius after the king’s death. Since women were completely dependent on their father, brother, or husband, they did not have much choice. In order to not be destitute they had to be attached. Even now women are poorer at retirement with less savings mainly because of missed years of income raising children. Social Security was partly founded to take care of these widows who wrote letters to FDR.

Chapter 8

  • “What happened to Julius Caesar?”: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He was stabbed in the Senate in 44 B.C. by conspirators including Brutus, his friend, and Shakespeare gave him the words “Et tu, Brute?”
  • “Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders”: Othello tells of “the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders” (Othello 1.3). The Cyclops is the one-eyed giant of the Odyssey, like one-eyed Beatrice.

Chapter 9

  • “the canker eats the rose”: “And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 35).
  • “all local habitations and all names”: The poet “gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 5.1).

Chapter 10

  • “his brother worm who was under the ground”: Job says “to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister” (Job 17:14), and Hamlet says, “Your worm is your only emperor for diet” (Hamlet 4.3).
  • “What is man but a poor, two-legged animal?”: Plato defined man as a featherless biped, and Diogenes answered with a plucked chicken. Lear calls man “such a poor, bare, forked animal” (King Lear 3.4).
  • “Porpoises shall eat the drowned sailor. The waters of this world shall close over his head”: The preacher gives the bride and groom a sailor’s burial at sea. Milton’s “Lycidas” (1638) mourns a friend drowned in the Irish Sea, and Ariel sings of a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies.” The line foreshadows Miss MacIntosh lost in the waves.

Chapter 11

  • “Pericles”: Pericles (c. 495-429 BC) led Athens in its golden age and had the Parthenon built.
  • “a society of night devoted exclusively to atheistic propositions”: “The school of night” comes from Love’s Labour’s Lost (4.3): “Black is the badge of hell, / The hue of dungeons and the school of night.” The phrase became a name for Raleigh’s circle with Thomas Harriot and Christopher Marlowe, men accused of doubting Genesis and God. In 1594 an inquiry at Cerne Abbas examined charges of atheism against Raleigh’s circle.

  • “we were the masterpieces of nature”: “What a piece of work is a man! … the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals!” (Hamlet 2.2).

Chapter 13

  • “Ben Jonson”: Ben Jonson was a significant early modern English poet and playwright, known for his satirical comedies, masques, and poetry. He was a contemporary of Shakespeare, received a royal pension in 1616 and is often counted as England’s first Poet Laureate, and is celebrated for plays like Volpone (a dark comedy about greed and corruption) and The Alchemist (a satire about fraud and human folly). “To Celia,” also known as “Drink to me only with thine eyes,” is a famous love song by Ben Jonson, first published in his 1616 collection The Forest.
  • “fixed like the North star”: “But I am constant as the northern star, / Of whose true-fix’d and resting quality / There is no fellow in the firmament” (Julius Caesar 3.1).
  • “my mother feigned death”: Juliet drinks the Friar’s potion to lie as if dead (Romeo and Juliet 4.1).
  • “not even the creaking of starlight”: Aristotle reports the Pythagorean answer: the spheres do make music, and people do not hear it because they have heard it since birth (On the Heavens 2.9). Lorenzo tells Jessica, “Such harmony is in immortal souls; / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it” (The Merchant of Venice 5.1).

  • “but what was a name?”: “What’s in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other word would smell as sweet” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Catherine says it of a servant whose name no one kept.

  • “Man was but a poor, forked animal”: Lear: “unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art” (King Lear 3.4).
  • “the fairest flower is plucked the earliest”: The Passionate Pilgrim (1599), published under Shakespeare’s name, has “Sweet rose, fair flower, untimely pluck’d, soon vaded.”
  • “still water runs deep”: “Still waters run deep” is a proverb of Latin origin now commonly taken to mean that a placid exterior hides a passionate or subtle nature. Formerly it also carried the warning that silent people are dangerous, as in Suffolk’s comment on a fellow lord in Shakespeare’s Henry VI, Part 2: “Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep” (3.1).

  • “Never married, never buried. An old man’s love is a young maid’s sorrow”: Both lines are old proverbs, often found in folk traditions and songs, particularly in the context of warnings against marrying old men. This phrase encapsulates the sorrowful and ambiguous nature of love explored in the book, especially the idea that some loves are doomed to remain incomplete, bringing pain and sorrow rather than joy. It also hints at the novel’s recurring motif of lost or ghostly loves that continue to affect the living long after they have faded from ordinary life.
  • “a fool’s paradise”: The phrase is Middle English, and the earliest known use is in the Paston Letters of 1462. In Romeo and Juliet, the Nurse warns Romeo not to “lead her into a fool’s paradise” (2.4). Miss MacIntosh tells Vera she was “living in a fool’s paradise, and now you know there is no answer.”

Young follows with “The true love wears an old shirt and is familiar.”
  • “where was Shakespeare?”: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet and actor.
  • “Watchman, what of the night? Who goes there?”: “Watchman, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11), and the opening of Hamlet, “Who’s there?”
  • “Out, out, brief candle!”: “Out, out, brief candle! / Life’s but a walking shadow” (Macbeth 5.5).
  • “we are sinned against more than we are sinning”: “I am a man / More sinned against than sinning” (King Lear 3.2).

  • “most men are conceived in the night and die with the ebbing of the tide”: In Dickens’s David Copperfield (1850), Mr. Peggotty says of the dying Barkis, “People can’t die, along the coast, except when the tide’s pretty nigh out.” Falstaff died “ev’n at the turning o’ th’ tide” (Henry V 2.3).

  • Classic metaphor for the fragility and brevity of life.

Malcolm tells Macduff, “Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak / Whispers the o’er-fraught heart and bids it break” (Macbeth 4.3).

Chapter 21 · Love as Eternal and Unchanging

  • “That love is love which… does not alter with the changing circumstance” echoes Sonnet 116, as in Chapter 18.
  • Vera emphasizes that true love remains constant despite changing circumstances. Love “does not ebb, does not wane,” symbolizing an ideal of permanence in an impermanent world.
  • This eternal love contrasts with the physical and emotional struggles depicted, underscoring a spiritual or emotional steadfastness.

Chapter 22

  • “it was a wise child who knew his own father”: “It is a wise father that knows his own child” (The Merchant of Venice 2.2). Telemachus says, “My mother says I am his son; but I know not, for no man knows his own father” (Odyssey 1).
  • “I know no Greek, less Latin, less Hebrew”: Ben Jonson said Shakespeare had “small Latine, and lesse Greeke” (First Folio, 1623).
  • “Here’s a horse of a different color”: “My purpose is, indeed, a horse of that colour” (Twelfth Night 2.3).
  • “those who fall in love are always blind”: “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see” (The Merchant of Venice 2.6).

  • “It takes more than clothes to make the man”: It means that a person’s character, personality, and true worth cannot be judged solely by their appearance or what they wear. A person’s inner qualities and actions are what truly define them, not just their outward appearance. This saying directly contradicts the proverb “clothes make the man.” Polonius: “the apparel oft proclaims the man” (Hamlet 1.3).

  • “Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green”: Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher, author of the Ethics (1677). Shakespeare was a famous British playwright.
  • “a sea change, a transformation”: “Nothing of him that doth fade, / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange” (The Tempest 1.2).

Chapter 25

  • “dead sparrows falling”: “One of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29), and Hamlet’s “There’s a special providence in the fall of a sparrow” (5.2).
  • “having been the jester with bells”: The court fool’s cap and bells. In Yeats’s “The Cap and Bells” (1894), a jester wins the queen only by sending her his cap and bells.

Chapter 26

  • “when we should have put off this mortal clay”: “Thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again?” (Job 10:9), and Hamlet’s “When we have shuffled off this mortal coil” (3.1).
  • “a bouquet of winter violets”: Ophelia’s “I would give you some violets, but they withered all when my father died” (Hamlet 4.5). Violets were a flower of faithfulness.

Chapter 27

  • “had died a thousand deaths”: “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once” (Julius Caesar 2.2).

Chapter 30

  • Childe Roland is a character in a poem by Robert Browning. The character Roland in the poem makes a journey to the Dark Tower much like the journey of Pilgrim’s Progress and the Divine Comedy. The name Child Roland comes from the Shakespeare play King Lear Act 3 Scene 4 Lines 195-197.

Chapter 31

  • “Life is but a walking shadow” - is a line from William Shakespeare’s Macbeth. It signifies the novel's existential reflection on the insubstantial, fleeting, and often bewildering nature of human life, where reality is elusive and individual existence may be more illusory than concrete.

Chapter 39

  • “Take arms against a sea of troubles” - is from Hamlet, Act III, Scene I the famous soliloquy “To be, or not to be.” The metaphor resonates with the novel's exploration of the ambiguous and often turbulent nature of existence, where the "sea of troubles" can be seen as the emotional and existential storms that engulf the characters. Taking up arms is a way of asserting agency and maintaining one's integrity amid the chaos.

Chapter 43

  • “Then put out the light”: This echoes Othello, Act 5, Scene 2, where Othello stands over the sleeping Desdemona and says “Put out the light, and then put out the light,” before smothering her in her bed. Several things in Cousin Hannah’s deathbed cries point to the play: she calls to a “Black Moor, beloved of woman,” she asks whether the turban-winder has come “to strangle me so that I cannot cry out,” and she lies in a bed that has become a deathbed. The suffrage captain, who spent her life refusing the role of wife, casts herself at the end as Shakespeare’s most famous murdered wife.

Chapter 47

  • “good-night, sweet prince” - Hamlet by Shakespeare. It signifies a final, loving farewell to a cherished figure who has endured great trials and is now moving beyond mortal existence. It reflects themes of mortality, transition, and the enduring nature of love even beyond death. This farewell is both personal and universal, blending sorrow with a quiet hope for peace in the beyond.

Chapter 47

  • “God rest ye merry gentlemen” - The song dates back to the 15th century and its historic meaning is “may God grant you peace and happiness” or “God keep you mighty, gentlemen” It appears in two Shakespeare plays and Charles Dickens’s, A Christmas Carol. It symbolizes a blending of mourning and celebration, highlighting the tension between mortality and the desire for comfort or joy beyond death. It underscores the novel’s theme that life and death are inseparable and intertwined, and that even in the face of death, there may be a call to continue the “dance” of existence, however enigmatic or elusive that may be.

Chapter 47

  • “I am the Ethiope” may refer to A Midsummer Night’s Dream by Shakespeare. The phrase is embedded in a passage describing various mystical and spectral figures, blending historical, mythical, and symbolic references. It reflects the theme of multiplicity and transformation of self, the blending of identities across time and space, and the difficulty of pinpointing a single, fixed identity or reality. The declaration “I am the Ethiope” symbolizes one aspect of this fluid, shifting self: an identity that is part of a broader cosmic and spiritual transformation, often with connotations of being an outsider or other.

Chapter 53

  • The “queen of the desert” who played pool may refer to Cleopatra in Shakespeare's play Anthony and Cleopatra where she is bored and asks Charmian to play billiards.

Chapter 53

  • The fighter retired from the ring and lived in isolation believing he had killed his father’s ghost when he killed that opponent. This is similar to the plot line in the Shakespeare play Hamlet where the ghost is Hamlet’s dead father.

Chapter 54

  • Lady MacBeth is a leading character in Shakespeare’s play, MacBeth. Lady Macbeth goads her husband into committing regicide, after which she becomes queen of Scotland. After Macbeth becomes a murderous tyrant, she is driven to madness by guilt over their crimes, and commits suicide offstage.

Chapter 54

  • Lord Banquo is a character in Shakespeare’s play MacBeth. He is at first an ally of Macbeth and they meet the Three Witches together. After prophesying that Macbeth will become king, the witches tell Banquo that he will not be king himself, but that his descendants will be. Later, Macbeth in his lust for power sees Banquo as a threat and has him murdered by three hired assassins.

Chapter 54

  • “My kingdom for a horse.” This line is from the play Richard III by Shakespeare. It reflects the desperate yearning for a way forward amid confusion, loss, and the labyrinthine journey through memory, identity, and the dream-like world. It conveys the idea of sacrificing everything for the ability to move, to find something lost (such as the bride’s skirt or love), or to regain agency in a disorienting and dreamlike existence.

Chapter 59

  • Mr. Spitzer presents a profound psychological and existential complexity that invites comparison to Shakespeare's Hamlet, especially in terms of themes of identity, death, and the nature of existence. Mr. Spitzer is deeply haunted by death and the boundaries between life and death, much like Hamlet. He reflects on the nature of his own existence, questioning whether he is truly himself or a substituted being inhabiting another's body and soul. This existential confusion mirrors Hamlet's famous soliloquies where he ponders mortality, the self, and what lies beyond death. Mr. Spitzer’s fears of losing identity, becoming “an echo lost under a domeless sky” or “a mirror,” echo Hamlet’s anxieties about the persistence of self after death and the fear of oblivion. Both characters exhibit profound doubt and skepticism. Mr. Spitzer doubts the reality of his perceptions and even the integrity of his own body, soul, and spirit, suggesting a “substitution” or a “temporary tenant” inhabiting his flesh and bones. Hamlet similarly struggles with uncertainty about the ghost’s authenticity, his own purpose, and the moral implications of action versus inaction. This pervasive ambiguity drives both men into introspective states laden with melancholy and philosophical questioning. Music, silence, and echoes play a crucial role in Mr. Spitzer’s experience, symbolizing the ephemeral nature of life and the haunting persistence of memory and death. He is “tormented by that echo which required the eternal silence and emptiness,” and fears becoming “an echo lost under a domeless sky”. Hamlet’s world is also fraught with symbolic resonance: ghostly voices, the “sound and fury” of life, and the silence of death. Mr. Spitzer’s silent music and elusive notes function as a metaphor for Hamlet’s struggle to articulate his inner turmoil and to find harmony amid chaos. Mr. Spitzer is burdened by the memory of his dead brother and by “beautiful memories of memories” that “thronged through his mind, as many as the dead”. This recalls Hamlet’s fixation on the memory of his father and the ghostly injunction to remember and avenge. Both characters are tied to the past in ways that complicate their present existence and paralyze their actions. Mr. Spitzer’s isolation is profound since he feels “porous as a cloud,” “disembodied,” and estranged from his own body and its skeleton. He is a “psychological beggar wearing a coat of patchwork,” a figure of alienation and displacement. Hamlet’s alienation is similarly acute, as he feels estranged from the corrupt world around him and from his own sense of self after his father’s death and mother’s remarriage. Both figures engage in philosophical meditations on the nature of existence, the self, and the cosmos. Mr. Spitzer’s reflections on the tri-stranded being (body, soul, and spirit) and the fluidity between life and death, suggest a mystical and metaphysical depth akin to Hamlet’s contemplations on fate, providence, and the “undiscovered country”. Fear is central to both characters. Mr. Spitzer fears losing his identity, the silence, the unknown, and the transformation into something unrecognizable. Hamlet is famously paralyzed by his fears and doubts: fear of action, fear of the moral consequences, and fear of death itself. This chapter reveals Mr. Spitzer as a modern, fragmented, and philosophically tormented figure who embodies many of Hamlet’s existential concerns. Both characters wrestle with the instability of identity, the shadow of death, the burden of memory, and the search for meaning amid uncertainty. Mr. Spitzer could even be read as a modern counterpart to Hamlet: an introspective, melancholic, and metaphysically troubled man who inhabits a liminal space between life and death, self and other. His ongoing struggle with identity, death, and the meaning of existence echoes Hamlet’s own profound dilemmas. Both figures exemplify the “tragic sense” of life, caught in a flux of doubt, fear, and the search for self-understanding.

  • The saying "Love is blind," meaning love makes people overlook faults, has ancient roots but was popularized in English by Geoffrey Chaucer in the late 14th century ("The Merchant's Tale") and later cemented in language by Shakespeare in plays like The Merchant of Venice, where it means lovers can't see flaws, even their own, and often highlights how love obscures reality and judgment, a concept supported by scientific studies on brain function during attraction.

Elsinore Castle is a real fortress located in Helsingør, Denmark.

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • “the depths of southern Indiana, a state as yet unknown to me”: Young was born in Indianapolis and lived for years in New Harmony, in the far southwestern corner of the state, where she wrote Angel in the Forest. Vera, raised by the New England sea, enters Young’s own home state as a stranger.

Chapter 3

  • Anabaptist groups are established in Iowa (Amish, Mennonites, Old Order River Brethren).

Chapter 3

  • The Protestant Work Ethic, the Calvinist Work Ethic, or the Puritan Work Ethic is a work ethic concept in theology, sociology, economics and history that emphasizes that hard work, discipline, and frugality are a result of a person’s subscription to the values espoused by the Protestant faith, particularly Calvinism. The phrase was initially coined in 1904-1905 by Max Weber in his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. Weber asserted that Protestant ethics and values along with the Calvinist doctrine of asceticism and predestination gave birth to capitalism. The novel is supposed to examine the culture of the Middle Westerner in the USA. It is defined by the Census Bureau as Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota, and Wisconsin.

Chapter 3

  • Miss MacIntosh's philosophy could be compared to the Amish, Quakers, or Shakers. The Amish have a significant population in the Middle West and are known for simple living, plain dress, and reluctance to adopt many conveniences of modern technology. They educate their children up to the eighth grade and then they are apprenticed to work.

Chapter 3

  • "Middle Westerner" encapsulates Miss MacIntosh's essential nature as a pragmatic, strong, and no-nonsense woman, deeply rooted in the values and environment of the American Midwest. The term "Middle Westerner" emerged in the late 19th century, solidifying a regional identity for the area between the American East and West. This region, often called the "Midwest," evolved through westward expansion and the development of transportation networks, particularly railroads. It became a distinct area with its own cultural and economic characteristics, influenced by both rural and urban landscapes. The Midwest, initially known as the "Northwest," played a key role in westward expansion following the Louisiana Purchase. As the frontier moved further west, the term "Middle West" gained traction to define the area between the Northwest (Great Lakes region) and the Southwest (Oklahoma and Texas). The development of railroads significantly shaped the Midwest's growth, facilitating trade and connecting disparate areas. A literary movement in the late 19th century focused on realistic depictions of Midwestern life, particularly in small towns and rural areas. The Midwest has been a significant force in American history, contributing to movements like the Granger movement (The Granger movement, also known as the Patrons of Husbandry, was a 19th-century agrarian movement that aimed to address the economic hardships faced by farmers, particularly those related to railroad and grain elevator monopolies. Founded in 1867 by Oliver Hudson Kelley, the movement grew rapidly in the 1870s, fueled by economic instability and the perceived exploitation of farmers by powerful industries.), the Progressive movement (The Progressive Movement was a period of widespread social and political reform in the United States, spanning roughly from the 1890s to the 1920s. It aimed to address the negative consequences of rapid industrialization, urbanization, and political corruption, seeking to improve society and government through various reforms.), and the development of industries and architecture. The Midwest uniquely combines urban industrial power with the conservatism of its rural hinterland. The Midwest continues to be studied and defined, with journals like the Middle West Review exploring its identity, history, and culture. The Midwest typically includes the following 12 states: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota, and Wisconsin.

Chapter 3

  • In an interview Young said she had no idea there was a real town by the name of What Cheer, Iowa. She thought she had made it up.

Chapter 4

  • “the promised land of which I had read in catalogues of wild flowers and seed catalogues”: The Promised Land is the land God promised Israel, “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8). Seed catalogues such as W. Atlee Burpee’s, begun in 1876, brought pictures of gardens and orchards to farm families across the country.

Chapter 5

  • “His hair had grown three inches since he left Persia at sunset”: Persia is a real small town in western Iowa. Midwestern towns often borrowed faraway names, such as Peru, Lebanon, Cairo, Moscow, and Athens.

Chapter 6

  • “though she had worked in a pottery”: Madge had left the town to work in a pottery or potter town that produced ceramics. In the Midwest through Ohio and Indiana, there was a variety of pottery and stoneware clays with common items made such as washbowls, jugs, and red roof tiles. East Liverpool, Ohio, which called itself the Crockery City of the World, is an example of a “potter town.”
  • “She was Abraham Lincoln’s sweetheart and Lincoln’s mother afterwards”: Ann Rutledge, Lincoln’s legendary sweetheart, died young in 1835. His mother, Nancy Hanks Lincoln, died of milk sickness in Indiana in 1818.
  • “it was not the malaria poisoning the air”: Malaria, “bad air,” or ague, plagued the marshy Midwest in the nineteenth century until drainage and quinine drove it out. It was carried by mosquitoes, not the air.

Chapter 7

  • Edward A Hannegan was a politician from Indiana. He murdered his brother-in-law in a drunken rage and was acquitted. He later developed a morphine habit as he continued in politics.
  • “It must have been that wounded bank-robber”: John Dillinger, from Mooresville, Indiana, robbed banks across the Midwest in 1933-1934. He had his wounds treated, and his face altered, by doctors who kept quiet.
  • “go over the river to the mines and be the paymaster, or he might dig coal in the pits”: Southwestern Indiana’s coal fields employed thousands of miners, who wore carbide lamps on their caps.
  • “The better element wanted to close down on old Josh anyhow”: Indiana’s county-option law of 1908 let voters close saloons county by county, and the state went dry in 1918, before national Prohibition.
  • “It’s awful the way these common people reproduce themselves”: Eugenics is an immoral and pseudoscientific theory that claims it is possible to perfect people and groups through genetics and the scientific laws of inheritance. Eugenicists used an incorrect and prejudiced understanding of the work of Charles Darwin and Gregor Mendel to support the idea of “racial improvement.” Women judged “feeble-minded,” like Musidora, were the chief targets of the sterilization laws, Indiana’s first among them (1907), and Madge asks why “the county” could not “put her away.”

Chapter 8

  • “where the cape of the glacier had reached”: The last ice sheets covered northern and central Indiana and left behind the flat, rich till plains.

Chapter 9

  • “What Cheer, Iowa”: A real town in Keokuk County. Its name is said to come from Roger Williams’s greeting to the Narragansett, “What cheer, netop?”
  • “a loving couple need not ratify its bond by marriage”: Common-law marriage, by living together as husband and wife, is still recognized in Iowa.

Chapter 13

  • “farewell to What Cheer”: What Cheer, Iowa, Miss MacIntosh’s hometown.

Chapter 18

  • “Oh, where’s What Cheer, Iowa”: Miss MacIntosh’s hometown.

Chapter 22

  • “cabbage roses such as grew, if not in What Cheer, Iowa”: Miss MacIntosh’s hometown.

Chapter 45

  • Twelve Miles - is what Mr. Spitzer thinks about putting on Cousin Hannah’s gravestone. There are some famous 12 Mile Markers in the US. There are also some in unincorporated communities in Indiana. It can also refer to a territorial waters limit. Twelve Miles can be understood as a symbolic measure of travel through life and time, marking a stage or a point that carries personal or spiritual significance in the midst of complexity and ambiguity. It is less a literal distance and more an emblematic representation of passage, progress, or endurance on the journey of life and memory in the novel's broader themes of time, existence, and spiritual quest.

Chapter 54

  • The Fishback Building may refer to the Fishback Company Building which was located on McCarty and Delaware streets in Indianapolis, Indiana. Frank Fishback started his coffee roasting business in the late 1880s and, by the 1910s, also sold Virginia Sweet brand foods including coffee and pancake flour. The Fishback Company closed during the 1930s.

Chapter 54

  • “Indeed, he had been offered, at various times, various railroads” The history of the American railroad system began in the early 19th century with early pioneers like John Stevens, leading to the construction of the first operational railroads in the 1830s, such as the Baltimore and Ohio (B&O). The system rapidly expanded, fueled by government land grants for transcontinental lines like the Pacific Railway Act, which connected the country by 1869. Railroads became essential for connecting newly settled areas, especially in the Midwest, with markets, fueling westward expansion and the industrialization of the Northeast. In 1862, the Pacific Railway Act authorized the construction of the first transcontinental railroad, which was completed in 1869, significantly transforming life in America. The federal government supported the construction of four additional transcontinental railroads through extensive land grants, encouraging economic growth and the creation of new towns. The nation's rail mileage peaked in 1916, with railroads employing a significant portion of the workforce. The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 established the first comprehensive federal economic regulation of railroads. Beyond these large-scale injustices, poverty, war, and the shortcomings of child welfare policies have also led to family separations. From 1819 until the 1970s, the US government and churches ran a system of over 500 boarding schools designed to culturally assimilate Native American children. The policy's stated goal was to "Kill the Indian, Save the Man". Children were forcibly taken from their families and communities and sent to distant schools. In 1891, the government began withholding rations and annuities from parents who refused to send their children. Upon arrival, children's hair was cut, their traditional clothing was replaced with uniforms, and they were assigned new English names. They were forbidden from speaking their native languages and punished for observing cultural practices. In addition to the trauma of forced separation and cultural repression, students often endured physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. Many died from disease or injuries and never returned home. Separating enslaved Black families was a common and profitable practice from the 16th to the 19th centuries. It was also an intentional tool used by enslavers to control and punish. At auction, enslaved children were sold separately from their parents and siblings, sometimes at young ages. Enslavers regularly threatened to sell off family members to prevent enslaved people from escaping or rebelling. Historical evidence suggests that between one-third and two-thirds of Black children were separated from their families during slavery. After emancipation, many formerly enslaved people spent years searching for lost family members. Between 1854 and 1929, the Children's Aid Society and other charities sent an estimated 200,000 children from Eastern cities on "orphan trains" to be placed with families in the Midwest. The program primarily targeted the children of impoverished immigrant families, particularly Irish Catholics. Many of the children were not placed in loving homes but rather treated as a source of indentured labor. Mixed reviews and the rise of foster care as a preferred method for placing dependent children led to the end of the program. During World War II, Executive Order 9066 led to the forcible removal and incarceration of over 120,000 Japanese Americans in internment camps. The forced removal resulted in the separation of families and shattered communities. Although most children remained with their parents in the camps, some families were separated, and others were put under intense emotional strain. The trauma of incarceration and displacement created lasting intergenerational trauma. Even after the closure of orphanages, children continue to be separated from their families through the modern child welfare system. Social workers often conflate poverty with neglect, disproportionately removing children from low-income families, especially those of color. In 2022, a Human Rights Watch report highlighted how poverty, rather than genuine unfit parenting, is frequently the basis for family separation. Black children, in particular, are nearly twice as likely as white children to be investigated by child services and separated from their families. In recent decades, US border and immigration policies have led to the widespread separation of migrant families. Under the Trump administration, a "zero tolerance" policy criminally prosecuted all adults crossing the border without authorization. This led to thousands of children being taken from their parents, often with no system in place to track or reunite families. Even after a court order ended the official policy, separations continued due to inconsistent record-keeping and a failure to protect asylum seekers. Pancoast, a professor in Philadelphia, took sperm from a handsome student in his class to inseminate an anesthetized woman without her knowledge. Her character is portrayed with a rich, symbolic density that reveals much about her internal struggles and her relationship to the world around her. Esther is described as physically large, often pregnant or swollen, with features like a long nose and crossed eyes, evoking a somewhat grotesque yet poignant image. She is burdened by repeated pregnancies, many of which end in stillbirths or miscarriages. This physical condition mirrors her emotional state: she is exhausted, confused, and isolated, caught in a cycle of hope and despair. Her body and mind are both "clouded" and "indistinct," reflecting her fragmented sense of self and history. Esther’s experience of pregnancy and motherhood is fraught with sorrow and complexity. She carries numerous "stillborn children," described almost as ghostly presences hovering around her, watching her with innocent smiles and applause, yet also causing her pain and distraction during intercourse. These spectral children symbolize her lost potential for motherhood and the deep trauma of repeated loss. She does not reject these children but claims them as hers, showing a profound maternal attachment despite the pain they bring. However, this attachment is intertwined with guilt and confusion, as she contemplates the nature of her past conceptions and births. Esther is entangled with a Chicago detective who is aggressively pursuing proof of his paternity of her children. This detective symbolizes the harsh, intrusive forces of society, law, and judgment. Esther fears his investigations, seeing them as threats that could expose her to legal and social punishment. Yet at the same time, she contemplates the possibility of the trial with a strange blend of hope and resignation, almost welcoming the exposure as a form of acknowledgment of her suffering and existence. This ambivalence highlights her isolation and the precariousness of her position as a woman burdened by reproductive tragedy and societal scrutiny. The chapter frequently returns to motifs of birth and death, conception and miscarriage, seen both literally and metaphorically in Esther’s story. She is described as knitting and unravelling a black hood, symbolizing the night and mystery surrounding her existence. Her pregnancies are "clouded," and her children are often invisible or spectral, linking her personal tragedy to broader cosmic or existential mysteries. Esther’s life is likened to an "empty coffin on the water," merging images of life and death, presence and absence. This symbolism situates her story within larger themes of loss, fate, and the unknowable forces shaping human experience. Despite her suffering, Esther exhibits a kind of wildness and defiance. She runs, she laughs, she knits, she endures. She is "wilder than people thought," living a life bounded by routine but also marked by moments of freedom and rebellion. Her laughter in the face of the detective’s threats and the looming trial shows a resilience and complexity that defy simple victimhood. Esther’s narrative is one of survival amid despair, of a woman caught between social condemnation and her own intricate inner world. Esther’s experience is deeply intertwined with natural imagery: autumn leaves, winter bees, snowflakes, mists, rivers, and stars. These elements emphasize the cosmic scale of her suffering and the universality of her predicament. Her children are likened to "snowflakes drifting in eternity" and "robed cherubim," linking personal loss to the eternal cycles of life and death. This connection to nature and the cosmos reinforces the mystical and tragic dimensions of her character. Esther Longtree is a richly drawn figure whose story encapsulates themes of loss, fertility, maternal anguish, societal judgment, and existential mystery. She is at once vulnerable and resilient, tragic and wild, caught in a liminal space between life and death, hope and despair. The chapter paints her not merely as a victim but as a complex woman grappling with profound personal and cosmic questions, embodying the novel’s broader exploration of human suffering and endurance.

The crime in question typically involves a situation whereby an intruder could not have left; for example the original literal “locked room”: a murder victim found in a windowless room locked from the inside at the time of discovery. Following other conventions of classic detective fiction, the reader is normally presented with the puzzle and all of the clues, and is encouraged to solve the mystery before the solution is revealed in a dramatic climax.   • “Death was birth, and birth was death”: Schopenhauer’s philosophy views death not as a final annihilation, but as the negation of the individual “will-to-live,” a fundamental force driving existence and causing suffering. He believed that life is inherently a state of suffering, a constant cycle of wanting and never truly being satisfied. Death, for him, is the end of this striving, the cessation of the individual will and a return to the underlying, impersonal Will. He argued that the fear of death is irrational, stemming from the attachment to the will-to-live. Although acknowledging the desire to escape suffering, Schopenhauer rejected suicide as a philosophical solution. He argued that suicide, like the will-to-live, is an act of will, preventing the potential for a more profound liberation through the negation of the will in death. His key ideas are will-to-live (the driving force behind our attachment to life and our fear of death), knowledge (shows the meaninglessness of life and the worthlessness of living), suicide (pointless because it affirms the will-to-live, though it destroys the individual), palingenesis (the will, not the individual mind or soul, is reborn in new beings), redemption (that death is an opportunity for redemption through the negation of the will). The passage reflects a worldview where grief and suffering are continuous and intrinsic to life. It belonged to an unknown prisoner who had likely been a student or traveler before the war. After ordering his ship, the pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee, to be scuttled in Montevideo on December 17, 1939, to save his crew, he died by suicide on December 20, 1939, in Buenos Aires. Hans Langsdorff chose to take his own life to prove that he acted with honor, ensuring his crew's safety after the Graf Spee was trapped by British cruisers. He is often cited for his moral courage and for prioritizing the lives of his crew over the strict, often suicidal, orders of the Nazi regime.

Chapter 2

Spinster was an honorary term for a woman who earned money spinning wool. They were regarded as “highly moral and fully womanly creatures'' and many documented in their journals that they “remained unmarried not because of individual shortcomings but because they didn’t find the one ‘who could be all things to the heart”.

Chapter 13

  • “the Venus was bearded by patriarchal fog”: Velázquez’s Venus at Her Mirror (1647-51), the Rokeby Venus, hangs in the National Gallery, London. On March 10, 1914, the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed it with a meat cleaver. “I have tried to destroy the picture of the most beautiful woman in mythological history as a protest against the Government for destroying Mrs Pankhurst, who is the most beautiful character in modern history. Justice is an element of beauty as much as colour and outline on canvas. Mrs Pankhurst seeks to procure justice for womanhood, and for this she is being slowly murdered by a Government of Iscariot politicians. If there is an outcry against my deed, let every one remember that such an outcry is an hypocrisy so long as they allow the destruction of Mrs Pankhurst and other beautiful living women, and that until the public cease to countenance human destruction the stones cast against me for the destruction of this picture are each an evidence against them of artistic as well as moral and political humbug and hypocrisy.” (Mary Richardson’s statement, The Times, London, March 11, 1914).

Chapter 30

  • A white skirt often symbolizes purity, innocence, mourning (in some cultures), new beginnings, versatility, symbol of femininity. As far as suffragettes they wore white as a symbol of the movement to represent purity and unity. The white skirt is a richly symbolic image representing a lost love, the ideal of purity and womanhood, and the spiritual journey through life, death, and memory. It is less a physical object and more a poetic emblem of the suffragette’s inner life, loss, and the mystery that surrounds her final moments.

Chapter 30

  • The white women’s suffrage movement, primarily organized and led by middle-class educated white women, focused on gaining voting rights for white women, culminating in the passage of the 19th amendment in 1920. The movement came out of the abolitionist movement with leaders being: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, Alice Paul, CArrie Chapman Catt, and Sojourner Truth (who played a significant role in the movement’s background). Suffragists employed various tactics, including lobbying, organizing marches and parades, and civil disobedience. After decades of activism, the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution was ratified in 1920 granting some women the right to vote. The 19th Amendment did not include women of color. It wasn’t until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 until all women’s voting rights were protected.

Chapter 30

  • Young's inclusion of women engaged in various sports and non-traditional roles for their time carries significant thematic weight. This imagery reflects the novel’s broader exploration of gender roles, identity, and societal expectations, particularly highlighting the contrast between conventional femininity and more liberated or unconventional expressions of womanhood. The detailed references to women participating in sports such as tennis, skiing, horseback riding, and even archery, as well as wearing attire adorned with sports motifs, underscore a break from the traditional, passive roles often assigned to women in earlier eras. These women vividly illustrate an active, robust female presence engaged in physical and public life, which was unconventional at the time. This challenges the era’s typical expectations of women’s domestic confinement and passive social roles. Miss MacIntosh’s advocacy for physical exercise such as bowling, horseshoes, and skipping ropes, and her disdain for luxury and affectation, emphasize a robust, self-reliant female identity that contrasts with the fragile, dreamlike femininity embodied by Vera’s mother, Catherine. The active, sporty women serve as a symbol of independence and agency, affirming a woman's right to self-determination and physical presence in the world. The references to sporty and athletic women suggest an ideal of physical health, vitality, and engagement with life, counterbalancing the decay, passivity, and dream states that afflict other characters. By incorporating women in roles and activities traditionally reserved for men, Young subtly reflects the social transformations occurring in the early 20th century, including the women’s suffrage movement and the gradual expansion of women’s rights and public roles. This is echoed in the figure of Cousin Hannah, a suffragette and adventurer who defies conventional female roles through her militant activism and boundary-crossing journeys, contrasting with the passive, isolated femininity of other characters. It also emphasizes the complexity of female identity. These external symbols of activity and engagement contrast with internal struggles over self-perception, societal acceptance, and the tension between appearance and reality, which are central themes in the novel. Young’s references to women in various athletic and unconventional roles serve to critique restrictive gender norms, celebrate female strength and autonomy, and reflect the complex, often contradictory realities of womanhood. They help to illuminate the novel’s central concerns with reality versus illusion, freedom versus confinement, and the evolving social landscape for women during the period.

Chapter 34

  • Through Cousin Hannah, Marguerite Young is not speaking about the futility of suffrage even though it was a long fought battle that has not been fully documented. In the book the Dialectic of Sex a quote from Carrie Chapman Catt estimates that: “to get the word ‘male’ out of this country 52 years of pauseless campaign… During that time they were forced to conduct 56 campaigns of referenda to male voters, 480 campaigns to get legislatures to submit suffrage amendments to voters, 47 campaigns to get state constitutional conventions to write woman suffrage into state constitutions, 277 campaigns to get state party conventions to include woman suffrage planks, 30 campaigns to get presidential party conventions to adopt woman suffrage planks in party platforms and 19 successive campaigns with 19 successive Congresses. Thus defeat was so frequent, and victory so rare - and then achieved by such bare margins - that even to read about the struggle for suffrage is exhausting, let alone to have lived through it and fought for it.” In light of this Cousin Hannah’s relentless energy is seen as not disproportionate to the women’s suffrage movement. Cousin Hannah’s attitude to marriage and men (at least the outward appearance) would reflect the fundamental struggle. Again from The Dialectic of Sex “To make both women and children totally independent would be to eliminate not just the patriarchal nuclear family, but the biological family itself.”

Stone loved the comfort and practicality of the outfit and wore it both at home and in public for about three years. However, the Bloomer costume attracted significant public scrutiny and ridicule, and critics of the women's rights movement often focused on the reformers' attire rather than their arguments for suffrage and other reforms. By late 1853, many prominent suffragists, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton, abandoned the Bloomer costume due to the negative attention it generated. Stanton persuaded Stone to follow suit. Stone resumed wearing long skirts, although she never again wore the restrictive corsets and voluminous dresses of the fashionable style. Other notable suffragists like Susan B. Anthony also stopped wearing Bloomers around the same time. Amelia Bloomer, the editor of The Lily newspaper and namesake of the costume, continued to wear it until 1858.   • The history of hyphenating a woman's name is tied to shifts in social customs, legal frameworks, and evolving gender roles. Initially, hyphenated surnames were primarily associated with the British aristocracy and were a way to preserve family names and inheritances, especially when there were no male heirs. Over time, the practice spread to other social classes and eventually to the United States, where it became a symbol of gender equality and a way for women to maintain their professional identity while acknowledging their marital status. In Britain as part of the aristocratic tradition, hyphenated double surnames were historically used by the aristocracy to combine family fortunes and affiliations through marriage. This practice was particularly relevant when a family had no male heirs to carry on the family name, allowing the name to be passed down through a daughter's marriage. Double-barreled surnames became associated with social status and prestige, reflecting the wealth and connections of the families involved. During the Victorian Era hyphenation gained popularity among the British upper middle class during the Victorian era, moving beyond the aristocracy. In the United States, the tradition of women taking their husband's surname was firmly established, with hyphenation being less common. The American suffragist Lucy Stone, who famously retained her birth name after marriage in 1855, became a symbol of women's rights and the movement to retain maiden names. Formed in the early 20th century, the Lucy Stone League advocated for women to keep their surnames upon marriage. The second-wave feminist movement in the 1960s and 70s challenged traditional gender roles and societal expectations, leading to greater acceptance and adoption of hyphenated surnames. Several states in the US began to make it easier for women to retain their surnames legally, removing barriers like restrictions on passports, bank accounts, and other legal documents. Today, hyphenating a woman's name is often a personal choice, driven by a desire to maintain professional identity, honor family heritage, or express a commitment to gender equality.

  • Coverture was a legal doctrine in common law systems where a married woman's legal existence was subsumed into that of her husband's, essentially making her a legal non-entity. Under coverture, a married woman (feme covert) had no independent legal rights, meaning she couldn't own property, enter into contracts, sue or be sued, or control her own earnings. This concept, rooted in the idea that husband and wife were one legal entity, with the husband as that entity, has significantly shaped legal and social landscapes, particularly for women. This concept formed the core of coverture, asserting that husband and wife were a single legal entity, with the husband as the representative. Coverture has roots in feudal Norman customs and English common law. It was a fundamental aspect of the legal system in early America, shaping social and legal norms. Coverture influenced not only legal practices but also societal expectations and gender roles. As the women's rights movement gained momentum, coverture was increasingly criticized as oppressive, leading to reforms. These acts, passed in the late 19th century, began to modify or dismantle coverture by granting women greater control over their property. Coverture was gradually weakened and eventually eliminated through legislation and legal reforms in the United States. While coverture is no longer in effect, its legacy continues to shape legal and social discussions, particularly concerning gender equality. Some legal scholars argue that vestiges of coverture persist in contemporary legal frameworks, particularly in areas like real estate and tax law. This resonates with feminist philosophy and critiques of power imbalances in society. Mr. Spitzer thinks all should vote, even the dead. This seems to be a call for the past to have influence on the present. The passage delves into the nature of reality and the interplay between the temporal and eternal. Mr. Spitzer's contemplation of the two moons, one "above" and the other "below," symbolizes a questioning of objective reality. His inclination to believe that the "sunken moon was real because it existed only in men's dreams" suggests a preference for subjective experience and the power of the imagination in shaping reality. This alludes to metaphysical concepts of idealism and the idea that reality is fundamentally mental or spiritual. The paragraph also touches on epistemology, the study of knowledge. The statement that "the mountain had not changed its snow conformations drifting through clouds, then the climber had changed," implies a recognition that our perception of reality is subjective and influenced by our individual perspectives and experiences. This relates to epistemological theories that emphasize the role of the observer in constructing knowledge. Mr. Spitzer contrasts himself and the woman, "He had stood still as she had progressed." This is implying the existential themes of freedom, choice, and the search for meaning. The woman's active participation in the world, her attempts to change and evolve, contrast with Spitzer's sense of stagnation and detachment. This highlights the existential emphasis on individual responsibility and the need to create one's own meaning in a seemingly absurd world. The concept of climbing old mountains as if they were new implies that existence is a continuous process of reinterpretation and re-engagement. The reference to the woman being "modern" and having "changed with the times" positions her as an active participant in the evolving world. This contrasts with Mr. Spitzer's being "stuck in the age of the surrey," symbolizing his resistance to change and his attachment to the past.

Chapter 52

  • The Swiss accusations against Cousin Hannah highlight the ethical problem of unintended consequences. Even if her actions were driven by noble intentions, such as seeking her lost love or advancing suffrage, they allegedly resulted in harm to others, such as causing snow-slides or burying trains. This relates to consequentialism, which evaluates actions based on their outcomes. There is a tension between progress and destruction. Cousin Hannah "uncovered some things" but "covered others," raising questions about whether progress inevitably involves loss or harm. This relates to dialectical thinking, where progress emerges from the conflict between opposing forces. The Swiss fear of Cousin Hannah potentially disrupting the stability of their nation reflects a conflict between individual freedom and the collective good. The Swiss are concerned about their community and way of life. This relates to political philosophy and the social contract. Mr. Spitzer questions the reliability of perception and the possibility of truly knowing anything. The mountains may be clouds, and the clouds may be mountains, highlighting the subjective nature of reality. This relates to skepticism and the questioning of empirical knowledge. The newspaper reports of the suffragette's adventures are presented as "blurred" and open to interpretation. This emphasizes the role of the observer in shaping reality and the difficulty of establishing objective truth. Mr. Spitzer's belief "when there was no reason for his belief" and his reservation of "his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others" suggests a rejection of conventional notions of truth based on empirical evidence or logical reasoning. This relates to philosophical movements like existentialism, which prioritize individual experience and meaning-making. The notion that Cousin Hannah's actions could cause "reverberations to eternity if not to infinity" implies a belief in the interconnectedness of all things and the far-reaching consequences of even seemingly small actions. This aligns with holistic philosophies that emphasize the unity of existence. The idea that "time and the dream were never married in her" suggests a rejection of linear time and an embrace of a more fluid, dreamlike reality. This relates to philosophies that challenge conventional notions of time, such as those found in process philosophy. Mr. Spitzer considers the possibility that Cousin Hannah might "ferry snow-crowned mountains of passage to another world" and "take all to that world where there was no mourning," suggesting a belief in transcendence or the possibility of escaping the limitations of earthly existence. These philosophical inferences are not presented as systematic arguments but rather as fragmented reflections that emerge from Mr. Spitzer's consciousness as he grapples with the legacy of Cousin Hannah.

Chapter 52

  • “that this old captain flying in her wasp-colored plane through the wasp-colored clouds over Switzerland had been attacked by a golden mountain eagle” - It symbolizes the struggles, dangers, and conflicts Cousin Hannah encountered in her life, especially in her efforts and battles for women’s suffrage and personal liberation. The image of the eagle attacking the plane in a wasp-colored sky suggests the intensity and peril of these struggles, highlighting her courage and resilience. The fact that nobody knew the outcome of this "battle" or whether she or the eagle had won or lost, adds to the mysterious, legendary quality of her character and story, emphasizing themes of uncertainty, conflict, and endurance in the face of adversity.

Chapter 52

  • “Perhaps he was like that Spanish don who, when his bride abandoned him to be the bride of Christ” - It evokes the image of a man whose bride leaves him not for another man but for a religious life, specifically to become a nun, symbolically marrying Christ. This metaphor reflects a situation of abandonment and loss, where the expected earthly partnership is replaced by a spiritual or unattainable one. Within the context of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer is deeply engaged in unraveling the mysteries surrounding the old suffragette, whose life and identity are filled with ambiguities, contradictions, and elusive truths. The reference to the Spanish don and his bride underscores themes of loss, unfulfilled love, and the elusive nature of identity and relationships. Just as the don’s bride chooses a spiritual path over a worldly marriage, the suffragette seems to have abandoned traditional roles and attachments, embarking on solitary, mysterious journeys and quests that defy conventional understanding. This simile highlights the emotional and existential solitude Mr. Spitzer perceives, not only of the suffragette but perhaps of himself as well, caught between realities, lost loves, and the search for meaning in a world of illusions and faded dreams. It suggests a profound sense of departure and transformation, where love is redefined, lost, or redirected beyond the earthly realm.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer's search through the house and trunks represents a quest for knowledge and understanding of the suffragette's life. The fact that he searches for "he knew not what" suggests that the nature of knowledge itself is uncertain. The "magnetic doors" that open on their own imply that some knowledge is revealed passively, not through active seeking. The idea that there were many differences between the suffragette's last sleep and her first sleep suggests a changing reality, shaped by experience and time. The "tumultuous life" alters the nature of her being. The reference to a "windowless seraglio or cave or darkened tower" relates to the mind as a prison or a space of limited perception. The idea of the "supernumerary love, a wife unknown" introduces the concept of hidden aspects of the self or unconscious desires. The paragraph delves into the nature of love and its mysteries. The "blind god of love" refers to the idea that love is irrational and indiscriminate. The image of the "turban-winder winding fields of consciousness" suggests that love can lead to a loss of individual identity and a merging of consciousnesses. The phrase "in the unwinding there should be no memory and no woman and no man" implies a fading of individual existence and a potential descent into nothingness. This reflects themes of nihilism and existentialism where existence is seen as meaningless and absurd. The individual's fading suggests a loss of self and meaning.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer's reflections are deeply rooted in skepticism and a sense of the limitations of human knowledge. The paragraph centers around the idea that "no language contained truth, for the truth was that which could not be expressed." This alludes to the philosophical concept of the ineffable or the idea that some experiences or realities are beyond the capacity of language to capture. This is related to mystical traditions and certain schools of philosophy that emphasize intuitive or non-rational forms of knowledge. The "word never written, the name never told" represents a truth that is forever elusive and beyond human grasp. Mr. Spitzer's "unretentive mind" is described as being "like a sieve," unable to hold onto definitive knowledge. This symbolizes the limitations of human memory and the unreliable nature of perception. This skepticism extends to the external world as well as he walks on and on "coming to no end", suggesting the world has no fixed state or endpoint. His experience aligns with skepticism, which questions the possibility of attaining certainty. The image of the suffragette reading a romance about "lovers never mated" (Eloise et Abelard) speaks to the theme of unfulfilled longing and the tragic nature of human relationships. Mr. Spitzer's inability to determine which character she identifies with (Tristram or Yseult) highlights the ambiguity and complexity of human identity and desire. The weighted eyes with pennies, "one in memory of the sun, one in memory of the moon," symbolizes the end of perception, the inability to see or experience the world, and the finality of death. The description of the world as "one level of sheeted silver and gold" suggests a flattened, perhaps illusory, reality. This relates to philosophical ideas about the nature of appearance versus reality, and the possibility that the world we perceive is merely a construct or a shadow of a deeper truth. Mr. Spitzer's reluctance to awaken the dead for fear they might die again connects the idea that it is better to leave things be than to interfere with the natural order of life and death. This connects to philosophical concepts of acceptance and the inevitability of death.

Chapter 53

  • “He knew a man who had fought on when he had broken his hand” - It is part of a richly symbolic and dreamlike meditation on perseverance, struggle, and endurance despite injury or limitation. Though the passage is metaphorical and layered with ambiguity, this particular phrase likely illustrates the idea of continuing to strive or fight even when physically or emotionally impaired, suggesting resilience in the face of hardship. Within the broader context of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer reflects on various images of endurance, loss, and identity, often blending reality and dream. The mention of a man who fights on despite a broken hand can be read as symbolizing the human capacity to endure suffering and continue struggling even when "broken" or diminished. It resonates with the novel’s themes of fragmented identities, the persistence of hope or effort despite injury or loss, and the ambiguous boundary between life and death, reality and dream. The phrase embodies the motif of persistence in adversity, highlighting that even with an injury that should impair one's ability, the will to continue battling remains. It serves as a metaphor for the characters’ emotional or spiritual struggles, such as Mr. Spitzer’s own wrestling with loss and identity, or the suffragette’s relentless, though ultimately tragic, quest for love and meaning in a shifting, uncertain world. The phrase underscores resilience, the refusal to give up despite damage or limitation as a theme central to the novel’s meditation on human endurance amid mystery and loss.

Chapter 53

  • “Death danced with the lady” This phrase metaphorically captures the intimate, complex, and ambiguous relationship between the lady (the old suffragette) and death. The lady is portrayed as someone who has lived a life filled with paradoxes, mystery, and transformative journeys. She is described as both active and passive, as a traveler between realms of life and death, reality and dream. The imagery of dancing with death suggests a close, almost companionable engagement with mortality, as if death is not merely an end but a partner in the ongoing movement of existence and identity. The "dance" implies a dynamic, fluid interaction rather than a static or fearful state. The lady, having abandoned conventional roles (such as bride or wife), and having lived a life of wandering, disguise, and defiance (including climbing mountains, flying, and escaping societal norms), engages with death not as a final cessation but as an essential part of her being and journey. It reflects her liminal status: between life and death, reality and dream, presence and absence. This metaphor also aligns with the novel’s broader themes about the blurred boundaries between states of being, the elusive nature of identity, and the intertwining of love, loss, and mortality. The lady's dance with death is a poetic way to express that she has been inextricably linked to death, not just physically in dying but symbolically in how she lived, loved, and searched for meaning amid illusions and truths. It signifies the profound and enigmatic connection between the suffragette and death, highlighting the novel’s exploration of mortality as a dance, a continual movement where endings and beginnings coexist, and where death is not a distant stranger but a close and intimate partner.

Chapter 53

  • “who vaulted the farthest distance” The phrase likely alludes to someone who has made the greatest leap (physically, emotionally, or spiritually) beyond ordinary limits or boundaries. In the context of the chapter's exploration of the suffragette's far-ranging adventures, both literal (mountain climbing, flying, traveling) and symbolic (crossing boundaries of gender, identity, time, and reality), “vaulting the farthest distance” can be understood as transcending conventional human experience or limitations. It suggests surpassing all others in attempting or achieving the impossible, going beyond the known world, or bridging the gap between life and death, reality and dream. This fits with the novel's recurring motifs of journeys through unknown realms, the blurring of reality and illusion, and the search for lost love or identity.

Chapter 54

  • The children kicking the skull on a playing field evokes a sense of innocence or youth interacting carelessly with death or mortality. It symbolizes how life and death coexist, often with the young being unaware or indifferent to the gravity of death. The skull, a universal emblem of death, is treated like a mere toy, indicating a cycle where death is a part of life’s play or perhaps ignored or trivialized by the living. This image resonates with the novel's broader themes of transience, the elusive nature of identity and love, and the blurred boundaries between life, death, reality, and dreams. Mr. Spitzer’s reflections on death, lost loves, and the mysterious suffragette’s life suggest that death is not an end but part of an ongoing, ambiguous process where the living and the dead intermingle in memory and imagination. The children’s act of kicking the skull could be seen as a metaphor for this ambiguous relationship, where death is present but not fully understood or feared; it’s a part of the world that continues in cycles. In context, it may also suggest the loss of reverence or the innocence of youth confronted with mortality, and how the past (symbolized by the skull) is treated by the succeeding generations: sometimes with disregard or playfulness, but always marking a connection between life and death.

Chapter 54

  • Bye, bye, blackbird - It is a poetic and philosophical meditation on the mysteries of a singular life that defies easy understanding, embodying themes of elusive identity, the interplay of dream and reality, the nature of love and loss, and the human desire to find meaning in the face of unknowability. Mr. Spitzer’s exploration of the suffragette’s estate and legacy becomes a metaphor for the quest to understand the self and others, a quest that is ultimately inconclusive but deeply meaningful.

Chapter 54

  • “mockingbird psychology” It is a metaphorical expression rather than a straightforward psychological term. Throughout the novel, there is a deep exploration of identity, illusion, reflection, and the blurred boundaries between reality and dreams. The "mockingbird" is a bird known for mimicking the songs of other birds, often symbolizing imitation, lack of originality, or an identity that is constructed from external voices rather than authentic selfhood. In this context, "mockingbird psychology" likely refers to a psychological state or pattern wherein a person’s identity, thoughts, or emotions are shaped by imitation or mimicry of others rather than originating from an authentic center. It suggests a kind of fragmented or dependent consciousness that reflects and echoes external stimuli or influences without a stable, original self. This fits with the novel’s frequent motifs of doubles, shadows, reflections, and spectral presences, as with Mr. Spitzer’s reflections on his own duality and the suffragette’s elusive identity. Characters often seem caught in a liminal state between self and other, reality and dream, original and copy. It can be understood as the psychological condition of being a reflective echo or mimic, lacking a fixed, authentic self, resonating with the novel’s larger meditation on identity, memory, and the elusive nature of reality.

  • A geographical pole or geographic pole is either of the two points on Earth where its axis of rotation intersects its surface. Chapter 54

  • “Indian maiden Pocahontas” Pocahontas also known as Matoaka and Rebecca Rolfe was a Native American woman belonging to the Powhatan people, notable for her association with the colonial settlement at Jamestown, Virginia. She was the daughter of Wahunsenacawh, the paramount chief of a network of tributary tribes in the Tsenacommacah (known in English as the Powhatan Confederacy), encompassing the Tidewater region of what is today the U.S. state of Virginia. Pocahontas was captured and held for ransom by English colonists during hostilities in 1613. During her captivity, she was encouraged to convert to Christianity and was baptized under the name Rebecca. She married the tobacco planter John Rolfe in April 1614 at the age of about 17 or 18, and she bore their son, Thomas Rolfe, in January 1615. In 1616, the Rolfes travelled to London, where Pocahontas was presented to English society as an example of the "civilized savage" in hopes of stimulating investment in Jamestown. On this trip, she may have met Squanto, a Patuxet man from New England. Pocahontas became a celebrity, was elegantly fêted, and attended a masque at Whitehall Palace. In 1617, the Rolfes intended to sail for Virginia, but Pocahontas died at Gravesend, Kent, England, of unknown causes, aged 20 or 21. She was buried in St George's Church, Gravesend; her grave's exact location is unknown because the church was rebuilt after being destroyed by a fire. Numerous places, landmarks, and products in the United States have been named after Pocahontas. Her story has been romanticized over the years, many aspects of which are fictional. Many of the stories told about her by the English explorer John Smith have been contested by her documented descendants. She is a subject of art, literature, and film. Many famous people have claimed to be among her descendants, including members of the First Families of Virginia, First Lady Edith Wilson, American actor Glenn Strange, and astronomer Percival Lowell.

  • “Penguin Colonization” refers to the process where penguins establish new breeding populations in areas where they haven't previously lived, often driven by environmental factors like ice retreat or the availability of suitable breeding sites and food sources. Historical colonization events, such as the post-glacial expansion of Adélie penguins in Antarctica, are documented through geological records. More recent examples include the successful colonization of artificial breakwaters by Humboldt penguins and ongoing efforts to establish new African penguin colonies to connect fragmented populations. Penguin movements, including the relocation of Emperor penguin colonies due to changing sea ice, are also monitored by scientists using satellite imagery.
