  • The Egyptian Sailor may refer to the “Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor”. A shipwrecked traveller engages upon a spiritual endeavour or quest, journeying through the cosmos, to meet a primordial god, providing to the traveller a gift of moral vision with which to return to Egypt. Further, Richard Mathews writes that this "oldest fantasy text contains archetypal narrative of the genre: an uninitiated hero on a sea journey is thrown off course by a storm, encounters an enchanted island, confronts a monster, and survives, wiser for the experience…” The tale itself begins with a framing device in which an attendant ("follower" or "the sailor") tries to comfort his master, who is returning from an apparently failed expedition and is anxious about how the king will receive him. (The Land of Punt was an ancient kingdom, likely located in the Horn of Africa, that traded extensively with ancient Egypt. It was a source of valuable goods like gold, ebony, ivory, and aromatic resins, which were highly sought after by the Egyptians. While the exact location remains debated, current evidence points towards a coastal region encompassing parts of present-day Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, and northeast Sudan. The kingdom's existence is primarily known through Egyptian records and depictions, particularly from the Middle and New Kingdom periods.) An attendant reassures him, advising him on how to behave before the king, and repeating the proverb, “The mouth of a man saves him.” To encourage his master, he tells a tale of a previous voyage of his in which he overcame disaster, including meeting with a god and the king. The tale ends with the master saying, “Do not make the excellent (that is, do not act arrogantly) my friend; why give water to a goose (literally, bird) at dawn before its slaughtering in the morning?” A Middle Kingdom text, "The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor," describes a star falling to earth, which led to the extinction of giant serpents on an island. This is sometimes interpreted as a folk memory of a meteorite impact as in the Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse. The sailor’s voyage appears to be a type of Otherworld Journey, a dangerous crossing-over to a divine or magical realm beyond the edge of the known world. “William K. Simpson observes that the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is ...one of the most interesting, straightforward, and yet puzzling compositions of ancient Egyptian literature. A curious emphasis is placed on numbers, the height of the wave, the dimensions of the ship, the number of sailors, the length of the serpent’s hood, the number of months of the sailor’s stay, and so on. It is almost as if the tale is an allegory involving the movement of stars. The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is considered to contain esoteric knowledge, much of it related to the serpent’s story. Whatever its meaning, this tragedy is enshrined as the central motif of the narrative: it is element X in a structure A-B-C-X-C'-B'-A'. Unlike all of the other motifs, its form is mythic rather than folkloric; it seems to be a religious allegory. As a mythic island (X) set in the dead centre of a sea of folktale elements (A-C and A'-C'), it may even be the “payload” of the whole story.”

The repeated themes of loss, desolation, and the finality of death align with Christian meditation on mortality, sin, and the hope or despair beyond life. This passage is a somber meditation on loss, identity, and the tenuous hold on reality, filled with symbolic and religious imagery that suggests a spiritual or existential crisis. Definition from research

Chapter 3

  • Coal mining labor history in the United States is marked by dangerous work, exploitation, and the struggle for workers' rights, driven by waves of immigration, the Civil War, and industrialization. Early laborers were diverse, including enslaved and free African Americans, and later, large numbers of immigrants from Great Britain, Ireland, and Eastern and Southern Europe were drawn to the industry by recruiters. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) was founded in 1890 to fight for better wages, safer conditions, and benefits, leading to significant labor conflicts and hard-won reforms like the eight-hour workday and pensions. The coal industry was marked by a series of violent conflicts and massacres, often stemming from labor disputes between striking workers (many of whom were immigrants) and mine owners who hired private security forces or leveraged local law enforcement to suppress union organizing efforts. Lattimer Massacre (September 10, 1897): In Lattimer, Pennsylvania, a sheriff's posse opened fire on a march of unarmed striking immigrant anthracite miners, mostly of Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and German descent. At least 19 miners were killed, and many more were wounded. The sheriff and his deputies were later tried but acquitted. Battle of Virden (October 1898): In Virden, Illinois, a gun battle erupted when the Chicago-Virden Coal Company attempted to bring in African-American strikebreakers with armed guards. Eight strikers and six guards/strikebreakers were killed. Ludlow Massacre (April 20, 1914): During a major strike in Colorado, the Colorado National Guard and guards from the Colorado Fuel & Iron Company attacked a tent colony of 1,200 striking miners and their families. The assault resulted in the deaths of approximately 19 people, including women and children, many of whom were burned to death when the camp was set on fire. Matewan Massacre (May 19, 1920): A deadly shootout occurred in Matewan, West Virginia, between Baldwin-Felts detective agency guards (hired by mine owners to evict striking workers from company-owned housing) and local residents, including the mayor and police chief, who supported the miners. Ten people died in the clash (seven detectives, two miners, and the mayor). Herrin Massacre (June 21-22, 1922): In Herrin, Illinois, a violent confrontation occurred between union miners and strikebreakers at a strip mine. After a gunfight and a subsequent surrender under the promise of safe passage, union miners murdered 20 strikebreakers and mine guards, and three union men also died. The incident is considered one of the most violent labor disputes in US history. Battle of Blair Mountain (August/September 1921): The culmination of the West Virginia Mine Wars, this was the largest armed insurrection in U.S. history since the Civil War. Thousands of union miners fought against local law enforcement and company-hired forces. Federal troops were eventually sent in by President Harding to quell the uprising, which involved the use of airplanes to drop bombs. At least 10 to 33 people were killed in the fighting. Columbine Mine Massacre (November 21, 1927): In Serene, Colorado, striking miners were met with machine-gun fire from the Colorado Rangers and guards from the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company during a strike, resulting in the deaths of six miners. These events, part of the broader "Coal Wars" (roughly 1890-1930), were pivotal in the struggle for better wages, safer working conditions, and the right to unionize in the U.S. coal industry.

  • Many young people served as soldiers in the Civil War, with estimates suggesting that around 10% of Union soldiers were under 18. Some were as young as 10 years old, and many served as musicians, messengers, or even in combat roles. While the official minimum enlistment age was 18, many boys lied about their age to join the military, and some were even encouraged by recruiters. William Black: At age 12, he was wounded in battle, making him the youngest known wounded soldier, according to Nashville.gov. Johnny Clem: He joined the Union Army at age 10 and became a drummer boy. Chapter 52

  • The 1850s and 1860s in the US were a period of intense national division and conflict, culminating in the Civil War. The central issue was slavery and its expansion, which led to political realignment, violence, and ultimately, secession and war. The decade of the 1850s saw escalating tensions surrounding slavery, with political compromises failing to resolve the issue and the nation moving closer to the brink of war. The Civil War itself, fought from 1861 to 1865, resulted in the end of slavery and Northern victory, but at a tremendous cost in human lives and national unity. Compromise of 1850 attempted to address the issue of slavery in newly acquired territories, but ultimately failed to quell the growing divide. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 introduced the concept of "popular sovereignty," allowing residents of territories to decide on slavery, leading to violence and conflict in Kansas ("Bleeding Kansas"). Existing political parties fractured, and new ones emerged, such as the Republican Party, dedicated to preventing the expansion of slavery. The movement to abolish slavery gained momentum, with figures like Harriet Beecher Stowe and her novel Uncle Tom's Cabin further inflaming anti-slavery sentiment. Dred Scott Decision (1857) where the Supreme Court ruled that enslaved people were not citizens and Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories, further exacerbating tensions. Abraham Lincoln's election as president in 1860, without a single Southern electoral vote, led to the secession of several Southern states. The Civil War (1861-1865) was fought between the Union (North) and the Confederacy (South), resulting in immense loss of life and widespread destruction. Major battles like Gettysburg and Vicksburg marked turning points in the war. Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared enslaved people in Confederate-held territory to be free. New York City draft riots (1863) discontent with the draft laws during the Civil War led to violent protests. The 13th Amendment (1865) officially abolished slavery in the United States. Reconstruction (1865-1877) after the Civil War focused on rebuilding the South and integrating formerly enslaved people into society. This era was marked by successes and failures in achieving true equality.

Chapter 52

  • The period from 1850 to 1860 in American news was dominated by the escalating tensions over slavery and the eventual outbreak of the Civil War. Newspapers played a crucial role, both reflecting and shaping public opinion on these issues. The rise of the penny press and the increasing use of correspondents, especially during the war, marked significant developments in the news industry. The debate over slavery intensified, with the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and the Dred Scott decision significantly impacting the political landscape and fueling sectionalism. Newspapers became powerful tools for disseminating views on these issues, often aligning themselves with specific political parties. The penny press, exemplified by newspapers like the New York Herald, gained popularity by offering affordable, mass-circulation papers with a focus on local news, crime stories, and human interest pieces. This shift in business model and content helped make newspapers a mass medium. While colonial newspapers were typically one-person operations, the 1850s saw a growth in the number of journalists and correspondents, particularly with the outbreak of the Civil War. The war itself became a major news event, with newspapers deploying reporters to cover battles and casualty lists. Newspapers were often heavily partisan, reflecting the political divisions of the time. They frequently supported specific parties or factions with editorials, illustrations, and even filled-out ballots and were actively involved in political campaigns. This contrasts with the modern ideal of journalistic independence. The telegraph, while not yet dominant, began to play a role in the speed of news dissemination, especially for major events. The development of the telegraph allowed for faster communication over long distances. Railroads carried thousands of newspaper copies across the country. The Civil War saw the rise of the war correspondent, a figure who would become a staple of journalism. These correspondents, including some who were soldiers themselves, provided eyewitness accounts of the war, often facing censorship and logistical challenges. Both sides restricted reporting and even shut down newspapers, causing tension with the press. Newspapers played a role in shaping public opinion on social issues, including the abolitionist movement. For example, Harriet Beecher Stowe's "Uncle Tom's Cabin", serialized in a newspaper, significantly influenced public perception of slavery. Western and Southern newspapers, often personal enterprises, emphasized local news, particularly about crops, land, and Native American relations. The Wide Awakes political organization, which arose in the late 1850s, relied heavily on newspapers to spread their message and organize supporters, demonstrating the power of the press in social and political mobilization. Legendary editors like Horace Greeley and James Gordon Bennett rose to prominence, shaping the landscape of American journalism.

Chapter 53

  • Archery - has been a crucial hunting method for millennia, with evidence of its use dating back to prehistoric times. Bows and arrows were also essential for warfare in many cultures throughout history. The widespread adoption of firearms, particularly flintlock weapons, by the 1800s led to a decline in the use of archery for hunting, especially in regions where firearms were readily available. However, archery did not disappear entirely. In fact, the 19th century saw a revival of archery as a sport and recreational activity, with the establishment of archery clubs and competitions in Europe and elsewhere. A notable example is the Toxophilite Society in London, founded in 1781. While firearms became more prevalent, archery continued to be used for hunting in some areas, particularly where firearms were not as accessible or by those who preferred the traditional methods. The "primitive" regions of the world continued using bows and arrows in warfare. Archery's cultural significance extended beyond its practical uses. It was often associated with spirituality, skill, and social status in various societies. The book "The Witchery of Archery" by the Thompson brothers, who took up archery after the American Civil War, is credited with inspiring a revival of the sport in the United States.

Chapter 54

  • “Indian maiden Pocahontas” Pocahontas also known as Matoaka and Rebecca Rolfe was a Native American woman belonging to the Powhatan people, notable for her association with the colonial settlement at Jamestown, Virginia. She was the daughter of Wahunsenacawh, the paramount chief of a network of tributary tribes in the Tsenacommacah (known in English as the Powhatan Confederacy), encompassing the Tidewater region of what is today the U.S. state of Virginia. Pocahontas was captured and held for ransom by English colonists during hostilities in 1613. During her captivity, she was encouraged to convert to Christianity and was baptized under the name Rebecca. She married the tobacco planter John Rolfe in April 1614 at the age of about 17 or 18, and she bore their son, Thomas Rolfe, in January 1615. In 1616, the Rolfes travelled to London, where Pocahontas was presented to English society as an example of the "civilized savage" in hopes of stimulating investment in Jamestown. On this trip, she may have met Squanto, a Patuxet man from New England. Pocahontas became a celebrity, was elegantly fêted, and attended a masque at Whitehall Palace. In 1617, the Rolfes intended to sail for Virginia, but Pocahontas died at Gravesend, Kent, England, of unknown causes, aged 20 or 21. She was buried in St George's Church, Gravesend; her grave's exact location is unknown because the church was rebuilt after being destroyed by a fire. Numerous places, landmarks, and products in the United States have been named after Pocahontas. Her story has been romanticized over the years, many aspects of which are fictional. Many of the stories told about her by the English explorer John Smith have been contested by her documented descendants. She is a subject of art, literature, and film. Many famous people have claimed to be among her descendants, including members of the First Families of Virginia, First Lady Edith Wilson, American actor Glenn Strange, and astronomer Percival Lowell.

  • “Civil War silver dollar” may refer to the Seated Liberty Dollar. The Civil War caused widespread hoarding of the coins due to their value. They were made of 90% silver. This led to a coin shortage in 1862. The government issued paper Demand Notes and later minted silver dollars which were stored in a vault for future use. The Seated Liberty Dollar was the design in use for U.S. silver dollars before and during the Civil War. A law in 1865 allowed the motto "In God We Trust" to be added to coins, and it was placed on the Seated Liberty dollar in 1866.   • “American soap flake king” may refer to Procter & Gamble (P&G), founded by William Procter and James Gamble. They were a pivotal force in the American soap industry and its transition to soap flakes. While British manufacturer Lever Brothers were the first to produce flakes commercially, P&G popularized the product in the U.S., particularly with its Ivory soap brand. The American Civil War provided a major boost to P&G's fortunes when the company secured contracts to supply the Union Army with soap and candles. After the war, returning soldiers created nationwide demand for P&G products. In the 1910s, P&G created Ivory Flakes, a shredded form of their popular Ivory soap. Before his candidacy for the presidency, he had been elected to the U.S. Senate by the Ohio General Assembly, a position he declined when he became president-elect. Grossman has stated: The question is that Quixote has multiple interpretations [...] and how do I deal with that in my translation. This is done [...] as Cervantes did it [...] by never letting the reader rest. You are never certain that you truly got it. Because as soon as you think you understand something, Cervantes introduces something that contradicts your premise. The novel's structure is episodic in form. The full title is indicative of the tale's object, as ingenioso (Spanish) means "quick with inventiveness", marking the transition of modern literature from dramatic to thematic unity. The novel takes place over a long period of time, including many adventures united by common themes of the nature of reality, reading, and dialogue in general. Although burlesque on the surface, the novel, especially in its second half, has served as an important thematic source not only in literature but also in much of art and music, inspiring works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss. The contrasts between the tall, thin, fancy-struck and idealistic Quixote and the fat diddy, world-weary Panza is a motif echoed ever since the book's publication, and Don Quixote's imaginings are the butt of outrageous and cruel practical jokes in the novel. Even faithful and simple Sancho is forced to deceive him at certain points. The novel is considered a satire of orthodoxy, veracity and even nationalism. In exploring the individualism of his characters, Cervantes helped lead literary practice beyond the narrow convention of the chivalric romance. He spoofs the chivalric romance through a straightforward retelling of a series of acts that redound to the knightly virtues of the hero. The character of Don Quixote became so well known in its time that the word quixotic was quickly adopted by many languages. Characters such as Sancho Panza and Don Quixote's steed, Rocinante, are emblems of Western literary culture. The phrase "tilting at windmills" to describe an act of attacking imaginary enemies (or an act of extreme idealism), derives from an iconic scene in the book. It stands in a unique position between medieval romance and the modern novel. The former consists of disconnected stories featuring the same characters and settings with little exploration of the inner life of even the main character. The latter are usually focused on the psychological evolution of their characters. In Part I, Quixote imposes himself on his environment. By Part II, people know about him through "having read his adventures", and so, he needs to do less to maintain his image. By his deathbed, he has regained his sanity, and is once more "Alonso Quixano the Good".

In poems Raleigh expresses a contempt-of-the-world attitude more characteristic of the Middle Ages than of the dawning era of humanistic optimism. Centuries later, William Carlos Williams added “Raleigh Was Right” (1940) to the conversation. It begins, “We cannot go to the country / for the country will bring us / no peace.”

Virgil wrote “Facilis descensus Averno,” “the descent to Avernus is easy… but to retrace one’s steps and climb back to the upper air, that is the task, that is the labor” (Aeneid 6.126-129), and Heraclitus, “The way up and the way down are one and the same.”

The Inferno describes the journey of a fictionalized version of Dante himself through Hell, guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil. In the poem, Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment located within the Earth; it is the "realm [...] of those who have rejected spiritual values by yielding to bestial appetites or violence, or by perverting their human intellect to fraud or malice against their fellowmen". As an allegory, the Divine Comedy represents the journey of the soul toward God, with the Inferno describing the recognition and rejection of sin.

It was written in the early 14th century. Allegorically, the poem represents the soul's ascent to God.

The term "courtly love" was applied to their relationship, a concept involving an idealized and often unattainable love that inspires poetry and virtue.

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • “because of a deaf musician” This figure introduces the theme of communication and isolation. A deaf musician cannot hear the music he creates or the world around him, symbolizing a disconnect or failure of connection, similar to the unanswered questions Vera faces.

Chapter 9

  • “A blind violinist and a deaf dancer”: There are many blind, deaf, and mute people in the book. This could be a play on the Three Wise Monkeys. The Three Wise Monkeys are a Japanese folk representation of the proverb “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.” They symbolize prudence and purity, and are often seen as a call for discretion or willful ignorance. The three monkeys are Mizaru (see no evil), Kikazaru (hear no evil), and Iwazaru (speak no evil). The concept originates in Japan, with statues of the monkeys found in temples and shrines. The proverb “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil” is often interpreted as a way to avoid negative experiences or situations by choosing to ignore them. In Japan, the monkeys are seen as attendants of Koshin, the God of Roads, and their message is used to teach prudence and purity. In the West, the proverb is often used sarcastically to criticize those who deliberately ignore wrongdoing. The idea of avoiding what is contrary to propriety is rooted in Confucius’s teachings. Some representations include a fourth monkey, Sezaru, who “does no evil.” One misses the train by seeing it but not hearing its whistle, the other by hearing but not seeing.

Chapter 13

  • “not even the creaking of starlight”: Aristotle reports the Pythagorean answer: the spheres do make music, and people do not hear it because they have heard it since birth (On the Heavens 2.9). Lorenzo tells Jessica, “Such harmony is in immortal souls; / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it” (The Merchant of Venice 5.1).
  • “a subdued roaring, a noise which came from the head only”: Tinnitus, a ringing or roaring in the ears with no outside source. Beethoven described it in the Heiligenstadt Testament (1802).

Chapter 29

  • Nietzsche’s frog is a way to metaphorically understand perspective and belief. Nietzsche believed that all knowledge and values are perspectival, meaning they are shaped by our individual experiences and values. This is reflected in the idea of a "frog's perspective," which can be understood as a belief system that is constantly changing and shifting. The term "frog's perspective" can also be associated with the idea of narrow-mindedness or being unable to see the bigger picture. Another metaphorical expression, "swallowing the frog" can refer to confronting unpleasant realities or difficult emotions in order to grow or achieve a higher level of understanding. This aligns with Nietzsche's emphasis on confronting difficult truths and embracing the "unpleasantness" of life. The frog can also symbolize a sense of "being in the muck," referring to the lower aspects of oneself that need to be overcome in order to reach a higher level of awareness. Frogs appear symbolically connected to themes of life, death, transformation, and communication beyond ordinary human experience. Mr. Spitzer encounters a mute man who uses a frog as a musical instrument, training it to croak and even mimic human speech. This mute and his frog symbolize profound voicelessness and the struggle to communicate in a world that is largely silent or deaf to certain truths. The frog’s croaking becomes an emblem of fragile, ephemeral voice amid silence, reflecting the broader motifs of mortality, loss, and elusive knowledge that permeate the novel. The frog also represents vulnerability and the liminal state between life and death. Its death mourned by Mr. Spitzer as a loss greater than many others. The mute’s deep grief over the frog's death underscores a shared human sorrow for lost expression and connection, heightening the novel’s meditation on mortality and the persistence of memory or spirit beyond physical life. Nietzsche’s frog metaphor, often interpreted as symbolizing awakening or transformation, where the frog must endure discomfort to emerge anew, parallels the frog’s role in the novel as a creature caught between states (mute yet singing, alive yet dying). The frog’s croaking in the mute’s mouth, its death, and burial evoke themes of metamorphosis, suffering, and the fragile boundary between existence and oblivion, which are central to Nietzschean philosophy of overcoming and transformation. It relates symbolically to liminality, transformation, and the struggle for voice and meaning amid silence and death. This aligns conceptually with Nietzsche’s frog as a figure of existential change and awakening, though Young’s usage is more focused on fragility, loss, and the ineffable aspects of human experience. The frog in the novel is a potent symbol of voicelessness, transformation, and mortality, echoing themes akin to Nietzsche’s idea of the frog as an emblem of awakening and existential transition.

Chapter 49

  • Young seems to use actual ASL sign language gestures but some seem to have changed over time.

Chapter 49

  • It also explores how perception and language mediate our access to universals. Mr. Spitzer's experiences as akin to a "blind man" or "deaf musician" symbolize the limits of human perception and cognition in grasping universals.

Chapter 51

  • “Seldom did he meet with anyone who did not suffer from some form of complex illusion beyond necessity” The paragraph begins by stating that most people suffer from "some form of complex illusion beyond necessity," suggesting a fundamental questioning of what constitutes reality. The examples of the old woman believing she's a birdcage and the piano tuner declaring foreheads "hollow" highlight the subjective and often distorted nature of individual perceptions. The recurring motif of blindness serves as a powerful metaphor for the limitations of human perception. The blind portrait painter raises questions about the nature of art and representation: Can true beauty or understanding be captured without sight? The reference to a blind war veteran visiting art galleries with a seeing-eye dog further emphasizes the limitations and interpretations of reality. The idea of deaf music critics "hearing" errors without actually hearing the music is paradoxical. It suggests that judgment and understanding can be based on something other than direct sensory experience, perhaps on intellectual analysis, intuition, or an awareness of structure and form. This challenges the conventional notion of sensory experience as the primary source of knowledge. Mr. Spitzer reflects that there might be "only one great dream informing all dreamers and all dreams." This concept aligns with philosophical ideas about a collective unconscious or a universal mind, where individual experiences are interconnected and share a common source. This also questions the nature of reality as an individual or shared experience. The paragraph questions whether time even matters when considering happiness. Is happiness something that exists outside of time, or is it bound by its constraints? The narrative suggests happiness is fleeting, like a snowflake. Time is further explored through the contrast between Mr. Spitzer and his brother. Mr. Spitzer's life has been so long that he can't remember certain things, while his brother's life was cut short. This contrast highlights the different ways in which time can be experienced and how it shapes our understanding of life and death. The observation that "three minutes of happiness seemed perhaps all there might be or less than there had been" in most lives suggests a pessimistic view of human existence. However, it also implies that happiness is a rare and precious commodity, to be cherished when it is found. The paragraph concludes by stating that "the greatest happiness might come through the sorrow of waiting, of postponement." This paradoxical statement suggests that the anticipation of happiness, or even the acceptance of sorrow, can be a source of fulfillment in itself. It also hints at the idea that happiness and sorrow are intertwined, and that one cannot exist without the other. The paragraph also touches on Plato's Theory of Forms. Plato believed that the world we perceive is merely a shadow of a higher realm of perfect Forms. The blind individuals, the deaf critics, and the deluded people Mr. Spitzer encounters highlight the imperfect and distorted nature of our sensory experiences. The idea that all dreamers share one great dream can be seen as a reflection of Plato's concept of the Form of the Good. This Form is the ultimate source of truth and knowledge, and it is what all individuals are striving to reach. The shared dream, therefore, could be interpreted as a connection to this Form. The paragraph reflects existentialist themes, particularly the absurdity of existence and the search for meaning in a meaningless world. The characters' illusions, their distorted perceptions, and the fleeting nature of happiness all contribute to a sense of the inherent absurdity of human life. Despite the seeming meaninglessness of existence, the paragraph also implies a sense of individual responsibility. Mr. Spitzer, as a lawyer dealing with the affairs of the dead, is tasked with making sense of their lives and legacies. This responsibility highlights the importance of individual choices and actions, even in the face of an indifferent universe.

Chapter 61

  • Deaf adults in research have shown a delay in seconds for visual cues and milliseconds for tactile cues.

Chapter 81

  • Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. One of the most revered figures in the history of Western music, his works rank among the most performed of the classical music repertoire and span the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era. Beethoven's early period, during which he forged his craft, is typically considered to have lasted until 1802. From 1802 to around 1812, his middle period showed an individual development from the styles of Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and is sometimes characterised as heroic. During this time, Beethoven began to grow increasingly deaf. In his late period, from 1812 to 1827, he extended his innovations in musical form and expression.

After recounting the stories of Esther Longtree, Miss MacIntosh, Mr. Spitzer and her mother, Vera turns her attention to her own experiences and a newfound love with a stone deaf man. This signals a move towards personal redemption and finding meaning amidst the chaos and illusions that permeate the novel.

Chapter 82

Since he cannot hear, their connection relies on visual cues, touch, and unspoken understanding. This echoes the novel's broader exploration of how people connect despite their individual limitations and the illusory nature of reality.

Chapter 82

He is bombarded by loud noises in his mind, but it is a silent world. Silence allows Vera and her lover to connect on a deeper level, transcending the superficiality of spoken words. The silence also seems to be a way for him to be closer to death.

Chapter 82

  • The stone deaf man's experiences also emphasize the importance of imagination. Having lost his hearing at fourteen, he lives in a world where sounds are memories or creations of his mind. This reinforces the novel's recurring motif of the power of imagination to shape reality and find beauty in the face of adversity.

Chapter 82

  • The relationship between Vera and the stone deaf man shows an acceptance for one another. He accepts that she can hear and she accepts that he cannot. This can be compared to the acceptance that Miss MacIntosh has for death and Vera has for her mother's opium addiction.

Chapter 82

  • The line between illusion and reality continues to blur in this chapter. The stone deaf man's perception of the world is shaped by his unique sensory experience, highlighting the subjective nature of reality. He says that life is imaginary and this is an imaginary world.

Chapter 82

  • Vera's loss of her pearls symbolizes the shedding of material possessions and the pursuit of deeper meaning. Her relationship with the stone deaf man offers a path towards redemption, as she finds love and connection in unexpected circumstances.

Chapter 82

  • The chapter explores different facets of love – maternal love, romantic love, and universal love. Vera's love for the stone deaf man transcends physical limitations and societal norms, representing a pure and unconditional form of affection. She feels elegiac even before her love arrives.

Chapter 82

Chapter 82

  • The final chapter reinforces the novel's celebration of the unconventional and the marginalized. Vera's choice to embrace a relationship with a stone deaf man challenges societal expectations and highlights the beauty of finding love in unexpected places.

Chapter 82

  • The final chapter suggests that the power of imagination and the capacity for love can transcend the limitations of reality. Despite the losses and disillusionments Vera has experienced, she finds solace and meaning in her connection with the stone deaf man, embracing a world where silence speaks volumes and love knows no bounds.

Clocks in this chapter are not merely instruments measuring time but serve as potent symbols of the instability of human experience, the blending of reality and dream, and the inexorable flow of time that ultimately eludes human control.

  • “the Big Ben alarm clock”: The Big Ben was the Western Clock Company’s alarm clock, sold from 1909 and the first alarm clock advertised across the country (1910). It takes its name from the great bell in London.

Definition from research

Chapter 12

  • “put his bet on the dark horse”: The phrase comes from Disraeli’s The Young Duke (1831): “a dark horse, which had never been thought of.”

Chapter 14 · The Black Coachman and the Family Carriage

  • Symbolizes continuity beyond death, the passage of time, and the family’s legacy, Catherine’s conscience and body.
  • The mystery of his grave and whether he was buried with his horses signifies Catherine’s fear of disruption and loss.

Chapter 14 · White Horses (King, Queen, Prince, Spade)

  • These horses have personified names and represent stability and tradition.
  • Their fate is ambiguous, mirroring the uncertainty in the narrative.

Chapter 14

  • “the four white horses”: White horses in mythology are often associated with the sun chariot, warrior-heroes, fertility, and an end-of-time savior. The white horses symbolize the solemn, mystical journey of the soul from life into death and beyond, carrying Catherine through the shifting landscapes of memory, dream, and existence by her will. They are a powerful emblem of transition, purity, fate, and the ethereal nature of mortality in the novel. In Revelation, “behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him” (Revelation 6:2).
  • “the barkings of spotted coach dogs running beside the wheels”: Dalmatians were bred to run beside carriages, clearing the road and guarding the horses.
  • “King and Queen, Prince and Spade”: The horses are named like playing cards, and the aces fall later in the chapter.
  • “the coachman was her conscience”: The Katha Upanishad: “Know the Self as the lord of the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.” In Plato’s Phaedrus, the soul is a charioteer driving two horses.
  • “driving a coach and six through a legal statute”: Attributed to the Irish judge Stephen Rice in the 1680s: “I will drive a coach and six through the Act of Settlement.”
  • “a horseshoe of white roses”: Floral horseshoes and saddles of roses honored racing men. Since 1932 the Kentucky Derby winner has worn a garland of roses.

Chapter 16

  • “The fierce, exultant pride that was mine”: In “What Is It with Women and Horses?” (Intelligent Horsemanship, 2019), Dr. Rosie Jones-McVey, drawing on her PhD research among British horsewomen, writes: “In Victorian novels, as well as in the more modern genre of pony-girl books, it is often aboard a horse that girls find their wings, often proving some snot-nosed boy wrong in the process, or enabling them to escape various romantic dramas and find solace in the barn. Just like the pony-girl books, many of my participants’ life stories entwined horseyness with coming-of-age stories. Horses were the means through which many women first acted in a truly independent way, often pursuing equestrian endeavours despite/without their parents, or else, proudly taking up adult-like responsibilities in being the teacher, pilot, and carer of their ponies, rather than the one being looked after and told what to do.” She argues that horses give many women a space for independence and self-assertion that their everyday lives do not.
  • “It was a steeplechase, and we would jump over all the church steeples”: The first steeplechase (1752) was a race across Irish country from one church steeple to the next.
  • “I was a bareback rider, wearing a plume, a pair of pink tights”: Philip Astley’s London circus (1768) began as trick riding in a ring, and the bareback equestrienne in tights became the star of American circuses.
  • “Falada could dance on his hind feet”: The levade and capriole of the Lipizzaners of Vienna’s Spanish Riding School, where horses rear and leap on command.
  • “served as a model for merry-go-round horses because of his grace in keeping all fours off the earth at once”: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed Leland Stanford’s horse Sallie Gardner and proved that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves at once, though not stretched out, as on carousel horses.
  • “the cabriole, the furniture of good Queen Anne’s day, whole forests of Chippendale”: Queen Anne furniture stands on curved cabriole legs, shaped like an animal’s leg. The name comes from the French cabriole, a goat’s leap. In dressage, the capriole is the horse’s leap with all four feet off the ground. Thomas Chippendale published his Director in 1754.
  • “following the movements of an imaginary polo ball”: Polo came to England from India with British cavalry officers in the 1860s, and Vera wears her “polo hat cocked back at a jaunty angle.”

Chapter 16 · Falada

  • Falada, the little black pony given to Vera by Mr. Spitzer, carries rich symbolic meaning that intertwines with Vera’s inner world and her journey.
  • Falada is described as an old, tired, wind-broken pony, light as a spirit, with a sagging back, a scrappy mane, and a knotted tail. Despite his physical frailty and advanced age, Falada moves with grace and seems almost magical, responding to Vera’s desires as if he were her own intelligence or head. The pony is said to be descended from a horse that inspired the jewel-studded horses of merry-go-rounds and carousels, connecting him to themes of childhood innocence and the cyclical nature of life and dreams.
  • Falada embodies a loyal, gentle companion who carries Vera through her internal struggles and the uncertain landscapes of her life. His responsiveness to her unspoken commands suggests an intimate connection between Vera’s mind and her means of navigating reality and illusion.
  • Although Falada is physically frail, he continues to carry Vera with grace and resilience. This mirrors Vera’s own vulnerability and strength as she faces the challenges of growing up and understanding complex realities.
  • Falada’s origin as a model for carousel horses evokes childhood fantasy and cyclical repetition, resonating with Vera’s oscillation between dream and reality. His presence blurs the lines between the tangible and the imaginary, reflecting the novel’s themes of perception and illusion.
  • Given by Mr. Spitzer, Falada also symbolizes a connection to a past that is both real and mythical, and perhaps a hope for guidance and stability amid chaos. His lineage to historical and artistic forms evokes continuity and the search for meaning.
  • Falada is described as seeming like Vera’s head or intelligence, suggesting that the pony is an extension or manifestation of her self-awareness and agency, her “headless rider” identity where the horse seems to guide the rider as much as the rider guides the horse.
  • Falada is a potent symbol of Vera’s complex inner life: her innocence, her challenges, her search for identity and direction, and the interplay between dream and reality that defines her experience in the novel.

Chapter 16 · Other Motifs

  • Falada represents freedom, imagination, and the link between past and present.
  • Moon and Stars are symbols of mystery, guidance, and the unconscious.
  • Marble Statues and Tombs are symbols of death, memory, and permanence.
  • Water and Sea Motifs represent transition, silence, and the unknown.
  • The entire ride is a metaphor for Vera’s inner journey. The horse is described as “almost only an idea,” and the house is likened to a tomb and an underwater castle.
  • References to historical furniture styles (Queen Anne, Chippendale), mythological creatures (phoenix, Triton), and fairy tales (the fairy tale of Falada, which Mr. Spitzer calls Arabic) enrich the novel’s layers.
  • The setting is a magical, moonlit garden and a grand, mysterious house filled with symbolic statues and motifs.

Chapter 17

  • “It was a horse ballet, a Spanish carousel with many mirrors”: Baroque courts staged horse ballets, and the carrousel was first a tournament of horsemen, like Louis XIV’s Grand Carrousel of 1662.

Chapter 17 · Animal Imagery

  • Falada, Vera’s old pony, a present from Mr. Spitzer, represents loyalty and alertness but is powerless.
  • Vera’s comparison of Miss MacIntosh to a “codfish swept up upon a barren shore” and “old man” adds to the grotesque transformation.

Chapter 18 · The Rider and the Horse

  • Metaphor for the unity of self and illusion, indicating the inseparability of dream and dreamer.
  • Vera wonders if she has “become Falada,” with Miss MacIntosh now the rider.

Chapter 18

  • “as if I myself had become Falada”: Vera’s pony of Chapter 16, named for the horse in the Grimm tale.

Chapter 22

  • “has won the famous steeplechase at Aintree where is the dreaded water-jump”: Master Robert, who had once pulled a plow, won the Grand National at Aintree in 1924.

Chapter 24

  • “Some had seen the black coachman”: The coachman and the white horses of Chapter 14.

Chapter 24 · Black and White Horses and Coachman

  • Black and white horses and coachman symbolize the passage between realms, possibly life and death, or reality and illusion. Earlier (Chapter 14) Catherine said the white horses were her will and the coachman was her conscience.

Chapter 26

Chapter 27

Its entrance is supernatural, blending reality and dream, reinforcing the theme of liminality between life and death.

Chapter 33 · The Black Coachman and Carriage

  • A mysterious child figure that embodies Esther’s ambiguous feelings about her unborn child and her fractured conscience.
  • Esther Longtree is a complex, symbolic character whose life and experiences can be analyzed in the context of the abortion rights movement in the US.
  • Esther Longtree is portrayed as a woman burdened by an "everlasting pregnancy," haunted by multiple stillborn children, miscarriages, and the symbolic weight of unborn or lost children. She is at once maternal and mysteriously barren, pregnant yet never fully delivering living offspring that the world can recognize or accept. Her pregnancies are often described as "clouded," "mysterious," or "stillborn," and she experiences isolation, societal judgment, and legal threats because of her reproductive history.
  • Esther faces accusations, lawsuits, and societal condemnation for the loss or absence of children, implicitly tied to notions of infanticide or abortion. She dreads being brought to court, exposed to public scrutiny, and misjudged by a jury that cannot understand her unique suffering and mystery.
  • Esther’s narrative is filled with ambiguity since she does not always know the fathers of her children, nor can she fully explain the fate of her pregnancies. This ambiguity echoes the clandestine and complex nature of abortion and reproductive control for women of her era, especially those marginalized by society.
  • Despite her "mulish" stubbornness and physical strength, Esther is powerless against the forces governing her body and fate. She is caught between societal expectations, personal despair, and the biological realities of her reproductive health. Her identity as a mother is fraught with loss, secrecy, and yearning.
  • The stillborn children and the "little shadow boxer" under her heart symbolize both the tangible and intangible losses women endure: lost potential lives, societal invisibility, and the emotional and spiritual costs of reproductive control or failure.
  • Esther’s fear of legal entanglement, the threat of arrest, and the impossibility of proving her innocence reflect the harsh realities women faced when dealing with unwanted pregnancies or abortions before legal reform. Her case is described as unprecedented, with no legal precedent to protect her.

  • The ravens appear symbolically and thematically as mysterious, almost otherworldly figures that contribute to the surreal, dreamlike atmosphere surrounding Catherine and her suspended existence between life and death.
  • The ravens are described as "two sister ravens who had created the universe" This description situates the ravens not merely as birds but as powerful, almost divine entities involved in cosmic creation and the shaping of reality itself.
  • Their role emphasizes Catherine’s immersion in a realm where boundaries between reality and illusion, life and death, are blurred.
  • The ravens, linked with creation, suggest a world that is constantly in flux, shaped by mysterious forces beyond ordinary human perception.
  • The ravens contribute to Catherine’s perception of her own life as “more monstrous than hers and terribly extra-human,” reflecting her alienation from the normal flow of time and human relations.
  • Their presence as mythic creators contrasts with Catherine’s physical stasis and withdrawal, underlining the tension between dynamic cosmic forces and her horizontal, dream-bound existence.
  • Ravens traditionally symbolize mystery, death, and prophecy in literature and myth, fitting well with Catherine’s liminal state caught between life and death, and her visions of phantoms, spirits, and the dead.
  • Their “sister” relationship may also suggest duality and companionship in a lonely, spectral world where Catherine resides, further personifying the enigmatic and haunting nature of her dreams.

  • Chaos theory is the study of how seemingly unpredictable and complex systems, like weather or ecosystems, can have underlying order and patterns, even though they are highly sensitive to initial conditions. It highlights that small changes in these conditions can lead to vastly different outcomes over time, a concept often referred to as the "butterfly effect". Chaotic systems are often nonlinear, meaning that small changes in inputs don't necessarily produce proportional changes in outputs. This can lead to complex and unpredictable behavior. A tiny change in the starting point of a chaotic system can cause a large difference in its eventual state. The classic example is the "butterfly effect," where a butterfly flapping its wings in one location might eventually contribute to a tornado forming elsewhere. While chaotic systems appear random, chaos theory suggests that there are often underlying patterns, feedback loops, and self-organization within them. Fractals, geometric shapes with self-similar patterns at different scales, are often used to model chaotic systems. They capture the complexity and irregular nature of these systems. Chaos theory has applications in various fields, including weather forecasting, fluid dynamics, biology, economics, and even social sciences.

The passage references metamorphosis explicitly and the transformation of earthly figures into ethereal or symbolic forms. This imagery aligns with the novel’s preoccupation with change, impermanence, and the fluidity of identity. The characters and elements listed symbolize various stages, states, and aspects of being, emphasizing that nothing remains fixed, and all life is subject to transformation. By mixing images of grandeur with decay, the list underscores the inevitability of death and the fading of all earthly glory. It stresses that all humans, regardless of status, are subject to mortality, a recurring theme in the novel. The cataloging of historical and mythical figures alongside ephemeral things like butterflies and moths, and symbolic references points to the fragility of memory and the losses that accumulate over time. Mr. Spitzer’s role is to navigate this complex legacy, but even he is often overwhelmed by the incompleteness and elusiveness of memory. The list contributes to the novel’s dreamlike and mythic quality. It mirrors the fragmented, layered storytelling style, where history, myth, and personal memory intertwine. This technique immerses the reader in the same blurred reality experienced by the characters, where time is non-linear and identities are fluid. The list is not meant to be read as a mere inventory but as a symbolic meditation on the themes of the novel: the passage of time, mortality, transformation, memory, and the intertwined nature of life and death. It reflects the complexity of existence that Mr. Spitzer faces as he attempts to make sense of the lives and legacies of those around him.

Chapter 2

  • Molyneux’s problem, posed by the Irish scientist William Molyneux in a letter to John Locke in 1688, asked whether a man who had been born blind and who learned to distinguish and name a globe and a cube by touch, would be able to distinguish and name these objects simply by sight, once he had been enabled to see. Chapter 12

  • “The eyeball was made to see with”: William Paley’s Natural Theology (1802) made the eye his proof of design: “there is precisely the same proof that the eye was made for vision, as there is that the telescope was made for assisting it.” The book opens with a watch found on a heath.
  • “dead men are usually found with their eyes open”: “Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes” (Genesis 46:4). The living close the eyes of the dead and once weighted them with coins.
  • “Leonardo had forgotten to give eyebrows to his Mona Lisa”: The Mona Lisa (c. 1503-1519) is a half-length portrait by Leonardo da Vinci. The painting shows no eyebrows or lashes, though Giorgio Vasari (1550) praised its eyebrows, “the manner in which the hairs spring from the flesh.”
  • “the garden of the blind”: Fragrance gardens for the blind were planted to be touched and smelled. The Brooklyn Botanic Garden opened one in 1955. Vera and Miss MacIntosh walk through this garden in Chapter 3.
  • “the stumbling stone to the blind”: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).
  • “the Braille texture of flowers”: Louis Braille, blinded as a child, published his raised-dot alphabet in 1829.

  • The ravens appear symbolically and thematically as mysterious, almost otherworldly figures that contribute to the surreal, dreamlike atmosphere surrounding Catherine and her suspended existence between life and death.
  • The ravens are described as "two sister ravens who had created the universe" This description situates the ravens not merely as birds but as powerful, almost divine entities involved in cosmic creation and the shaping of reality itself.
  • Their role emphasizes Catherine’s immersion in a realm where boundaries between reality and illusion, life and death, are blurred.
  • The ravens, linked with creation, suggest a world that is constantly in flux, shaped by mysterious forces beyond ordinary human perception.
  • The ravens contribute to Catherine’s perception of her own life as “more monstrous than hers and terribly extra-human,” reflecting her alienation from the normal flow of time and human relations.
  • Their presence as mythic creators contrasts with Catherine’s physical stasis and withdrawal, underlining the tension between dynamic cosmic forces and her horizontal, dream-bound existence.
  • Ravens traditionally symbolize mystery, death, and prophecy in literature and myth, fitting well with Catherine’s liminal state caught between life and death, and her visions of phantoms, spirits, and the dead.
  • Their “sister” relationship may also suggest duality and companionship in a lonely, spectral world where Catherine resides, further personifying the enigmatic and haunting nature of her dreams.

Chapter 3

  • “all these fine-feathered birds of paradise”: The birds of paradise of New Guinea reached Europe in the 1500s as trade skins with their feet removed, and naturalists concluded that they had no feet and lived their whole lives in the air, feeding on dew, until they fell to earth at death. Linnaeus named one species Paradisaea apoda, “footless.”
  • “an Arctic tern stopping upon the rocks”: The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying each year from its Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back, and so sees two summers and more daylight than any other creature.

  • Symbolizes vitality, passion, and the vividness of Miss MacIntosh’s presence.

  • Symbolizes fragile consciousness, the artificiality of appearance, and the precariousness of Madge’s situation.

Chapter 6

  • “little red-winged blackbirds where the snow was falling”: Blackbirds can symbolize different things depending on the culture: death, change, magic, and mystery. Specifically in Christianity it is a symbol of temptation and carnal pleasure. Blackbirds in the chapter are multifaceted symbols embodying death, the haunting past, sorrow, and the thin veil separating life and death, reinforcing the novel’s pervasive atmosphere of melancholy and existential uncertainty.

Chapter 9 · Bird Imagery, Especially Seagulls

  • Seagulls appear as recurring natural motifs connected with care and injury. They may symbolize vulnerability and healing, but also freedom and the natural world.
  • The death of the seagull “when its wound was healed” suggests a paradox of survival and loss, or the cost of recovery.

Chapter 11

  • “Queen Charlotte Islands”: The Queen Charlotte Islands, off the Pacific coast of Canada, were named in 1787 for the ship Queen Charlotte, which was named for George III’s queen. They are the home of the Haida and are now called Haida Gwaii.
  • “a wild swan absent, one wild swan more”: In Andersen’s “The Wild Swans” (1838), eleven brothers are turned into swans, and their sister weaves nettle shirts to free them. The last shirt is unfinished, and the youngest is left with a swan’s wing.
  • “the sister ravens, the brother doves”: The Grimms’ “The Seven Ravens” and Giambattista Basile’s “The Seven Doves” (1634-36) both tell of brothers changed into birds and a sister who saves them. Young makes the ravens sisters.

Chapter 12

  • “the spot on a peacock’s tail”: Juno set the hundred eyes of the slain watchman Argus in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).
  • “Mr. Chandelier or Mr. Chanticleer”: Chanticleer is the proud rooster of Chaucer’s “The Nun’s Priest’s Tale” and the fables of Reynard the Fox. Mr. Chandelier is Catherine’s companion from Chapter 2.
  • “a rooster crowing when there was no rooster”: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Matthew 26:34).
  • “twelve white swans like brothers or suitors bewitched”: Andersen’s eleven brothers turned into swans, and the bewitched swan maidens of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877).

Chapter 13

  • “One should see the bird and the shadow of the bird, but one should not hear the song”: Wallace Stevens, “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird” (1917): “The blackbird whistling / Or just after.”

Chapter 14

  • “the golden cock perched at the foot of her bed, that it was really Pythagoras shedding his golden feathers”: In Lucian’s dialogue “The Dream, or the Cock,” a cobbler’s rooster reveals that it is Pythagoras reborn. Pythagoras was said to have a golden thigh. Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera The Golden Cockerel (1909), from Pushkin’s tale (1834), has a golden cock that warns a tsar.
  • “her peacocks”: Aristotle referred to the peacock’s vain reputation. The Roman poet Ennius, following the Pythagorean teaching of rebirth, dreamed that Homer’s soul had passed into a peacock and then into himself. The peacock symbolizes the dazzling but ephemeral nature of beauty and social display, the multiplicity and fragmentation of perception, and the tension between illusion and reality that the characters navigate.

Chapter 16

Chapter 18 · Feather Pillow

Chapter 27

  • “storks’ nests on the roof-tops”: In northern Europe a stork’s nest on the roof brought luck, and storks brought babies. Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Storks” (1838).

Chapter 72 · The pearl-like raindrops that never fall

  • Reflect suspended time and unfulfilled potential.
  • Esther Longtree may symbolize the sexual revolution in the United States by considering her character’s embodiment of themes such as fertility, sexuality, societal repression, and the struggle for female autonomy.
  • Esther is depicted as "everlastingly pregnant," carrying multiple stillborn children, representing an ongoing, unresolved fertility and reproductive issue. She is physically swollen, with symptoms of pregnancy (morning sickness, evening sickness, swollen breasts) but no viable birth occurs. This paradox of constant pregnancy without fulfillment can symbolize the tension in the 1960s between traditional expectations of women centered on motherhood and the emerging desire for sexual freedom and reproductive control. Esther’s "everlasting pregnancy" may reflect the societal burden placed on women to reproduce and the frustration when that role is unfulfilled or controlled by external forces like sterile fathers or societal norms.
  • Esther is described as robustly alive and free in some ways like her hair that flows loose "at whatever cost to sanitation," and she tosses it regularly as if to preserve her freedom. This image evokes a woman resisting social constraints, symbolic of the sexual liberation movement where women began to assert control over their own bodies and sexuality. Yet, she is also trapped in a "womb" that is both a restaurant and a grave, a liminal space between life and death, fertility and barrenness, reflecting the societal repression of female sexuality and the stigma around pregnancy out of wedlock or outside accepted norms.
  • The numerous stillborn children Esther carries (hidden under leaves, buds, snow, rivers) represent unrealized potential, lost possibilities, and the silencing of female sexual and reproductive expression. The fact that the fathers are "sterile" or "impotent" men, often traveling salesmen or transient figures, can symbolize the failure of patriarchal structures to support or recognize women's full sexual agency. The stillborns haunt Esther, much like the repressed desires and consequences of sexual control haunt society during the sexual revolution.
  • Esther is simultaneously described as "brilliant but dumb," "ugly outside... but beautiful inside," "experienced and sought after" yet also an "old maid" misunderstood by her own parents. This duality reflects the conflicted social status of women during this time who were beginning to break free from traditional roles but still faced judgment, misunderstanding, and marginalization. Esther’s education and cultural refinement contrast with her physical and social marginalization, symbolizing the new woman’s struggle to reconcile intellect, sexuality, and societal acceptance.
  • Esther’s "immortal medical case" status, with the old doctor predicting she will "be pregnant until the stars had fallen," suggests the ongoing, unresolved nature of women’s sexual liberation. The "everlasting pregnancy" can metaphorically represent the period of social transformation as an era pregnant with possibilities but fraught with struggle, loss, and hope. Her hopefulness despite repeated disappointments mirrors the spirit of the sexual revolution, which challenged existing norms and sought new forms of expression and liberation.
  • Her affinity with natural and mythical elements (wild mares pregnant by the wind, the great skull, the starry heavens, the moon, and the stars) links Esther to a broader symbolic framework of fertility, creation, and cosmic forces. This elevates her personal reproductive tragedy to a universal level, reflecting the countercultural embrace of naturalism, mysticism, and a redefinition of human sexuality as part of a cosmic order or liberation from mechanistic, repressive traditions.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes the complexities and contradictions of the sexual revolution in America: the tension between fertility and barrenness, freedom and repression, hope and despair, tradition and change. Her character embodies the social anxieties about female sexuality, the quest for autonomy, and the redefinition of womanhood during a period of profound cultural upheaval.
  • Her story encapsulates the bodily, social, and legal struggles over reproduction, economic survival, and patriarchal oppression that shaped the conditions the women’s rights movement sought to change through activism.

From the resources

Chapter 2

  • Pearl-divers recover pearls from wild mollusks (oysters or mussels) in the sea or fresh-water.
  • Pearls symbolize wisdom acquired through experience, purity, generosity, integrity, and loyalty. They are believed to attract wealth and luck as well as offer protection.

Chapter 51

  • “nacreous” Nacreous means resembling or having the appearance of mother-of-pearl; lustrous and iridescent. It describes something that has a pearly, shimmering quality, often with a play of colors like a rainbow.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer's meticulous accounting and listing is directly tied to his struggle with his identity, particularly his relationship with his deceased brother. He seeks a perfect balance, a mirrored reflection where everything in his life corresponds to his brother's, suggesting a desire to understand himself through this dualistic lens. The fear of "no differing counterpart" speaks to the existential anxiety of lacking a defined self, relying on another for definition. This resonates with philosophical concepts of identity formation, the "self" versus the "other," and the influence of external relationships on self-perception. Thinkers like Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir explored similar themes in existentialism. Spitzer's obsessive listing and indexing of even the most mundane objects (pearl buttons, rusted nail heads, etc.) reflects a deep-seated need to impose order on a chaotic world. He's trying to find patterns, connections, and a "common denominator" to make sense of existence. This aligns with the philosophical pursuit of metaphysics: trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality. The futility of Spitzer's efforts mirrors the inherent difficulties in finding absolute order or meaning in a world often perceived as absurd or chaotic (a key theme in existentialism and absurdism). The questions about the sail ("Was the sail unwinding the same as the winding sail?") touch on the philosophical problem of identity over time. Does something remain the same if its state changes? This is further complicated by the cyclical nature of the tides and the wagon wheels, implying a sense of eternal return or repetition. This connects to Heraclitus's famous saying, "No man ever steps in the same river twice," emphasizing the constant flux and change in the universe. The paragraph also hints at Nietzsche's concept of eternal recurrence. Spitzer's attempts to capture reality through lists and measurements are ultimately limited. His fear that "all the weight, as he had often complained, was on this weightless star" alludes to the disparity between the tangible and intangible, the concrete and abstract. He can list the physical properties of objects, but he cannot capture their essence or meaning. This is related to epistemology, the study of knowledge and its limitations. The paragraph suggests the impossibility of fully knowing or representing reality, as there will always be something missing or lost in translation. The description of Spitzer's actions creating "division as in division there was creation," suggests that in every act of creation, there is also an act of destruction. This mirrors the belief that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. This is connected to the concept of the "Tao" which states that everything is composed of two opposites, and that without the other, it cannot exist.

Chapter 55

  • “mother-of-pearl Venus comb” is a species of large predatory sea snail, a marine gastropod mollusk in the family Muricidae, the rock snails or murex snails. The shell of this Indo-Pacific species has a very long siphonal canal and numerous spines. Perfect specimens of the shell are not easily found because of the fragility of the numerous long spines.

Chapter 58

  • Pearl-buttoned spats were a popular, elegant fashion accessory for both men and women from the late 19th century to the 1920s. Originally designed to protect footwear from dirt on unpaved roads, they became a symbol of social status and high fashion, especially during the Victorian and Edwardian eras. The trend began to fade in the late 1920s with the rise of more casual styles and shorter hemlines, which made intricate footwear and decorative buttons more visible.

Chapter 63

  • King Canute or Cnut was king of England, Norway, and Denmark. Miss MacIntosh invokes King Canute, who commanded the tides to stop, to illustrate the futility of "waste our lives in the vain expectation of that which might never happen". Canute, who despite being king, could not control the natural world, serves as a reminder that one must not dream of "what was not, of what would never be". He represents the limitations of human power against the forces of nature and the folly of arrogance. Catherine also mentions King Canute when she is lost in her opium-induced dreams. This further connects him with the realm of illusion and the rejection of reality that Miss MacIntosh so vehemently opposes. The story notes her mention of the "drowned pearl-diver rising to the surface, the griffin with folded wings, the centaur with its long-lashed eyelids closed," alongside her comment that James, the chauffeur, could be depended upon. Miss MacIntosh is said to be able to "do away with bodiless phantoms and monsters, with imaginary nightingales or turrets of ivory or turrets of gold or turrets of brass". King Canute, as used by Miss MacIntosh, directly contrasts with Catherine's "opium paradise." He embodies the futility of attempting to control the uncontrollable, while Vera's mother indulges in dreams that defy reality. Miss MacIntosh emphasizes that the "opium paradise was never God's way of life". The references to King Canute, particularly by Miss MacIntosh, serve as a critique of those who dwell in idealistic or unrealistic notions. He is a symbol of misplaced faith in one's ability to alter the fundamental realities of the world.

Chapter 71

  • The pearls are repeatedly connected to Vera's mother and her legacy. They represent the "lost estate" of her mother, something precious yet intangible that Vera inherits and wears, symbolizing the remnants of the past and the enduring connection to her mother's life and identity. The pearls are described as "real pearls which... would bring no more than cultivated pearls" in the market, suggesting a contrast between their material and symbolic value. The pearls also symbolize continuity amid loss and the passing of time. Vera’s mother believed that the pearls could not be lost or stolen, and that their number paradoxically increased with loss, implying an infinite or eternal quality beyond physical reality. This suggests a theme of immortality or persistence beyond death, where loss in one sense begets gain in another "the more pearls there were" despite losses in life. The novel often blurs the line between dream and reality, and pearls, like many other images, are part of this interplay. Pearls are associated with the ephemeral and the eternal, with illusions and truths mingling. They appear alongside motifs of opium dreams, ghosts, and phantoms, symbolizing the fragile and shifting nature of existence and memory. The pearls are linked to the theme of identity, as something that persists yet changes, much like Vera’s mother herself, who is simultaneously present and absent, real and dreamlike. The pearls become a metaphor for what remains of a person’s essence when all else has faded or been lost. The imagery of pearls dripping or cascading like tears, linked to the mother’s lifeless but radiant hands, suggests mourning and the cycle of life and death. Pearls are connected to sorrow ("the pity, pity, pity of nothing, of something"), highlighting their role as symbols of grief and the preciousness of what is gone.

Chapter 82

  • Vera's loss of her pearls symbolizes the shedding of material possessions and the pursuit of deeper meaning. Her relationship with the stone deaf man offers a path towards redemption, as she finds love and connection in unexpected circumstances.

Chapter 4 · Nature’s Cruelty and Funeral Wreaths

  • The natural world is depicted not as nurturing but cold and indifferent.

Chapter 6 · The Wedding and Funeral Imagery

  • Madge’s “wedding” is a funeral; marriage equals death in her experience.
  • The absence of traditional wedding symbols intensifies the sense of loss and unrealized hopes.

Chapter 6

  • “until Death did them part”: The phrase comes from the marriage vows of the Book of Common Prayer (1549), which read “till death us depart”; the wording later became “till death us do part.” The same vows promise “for better for worse.”
  • “her little wedding cake bridegroom with his polished mustache”: Cake toppers of a tiny bride and groom became fashionable in the United States in the early twentieth century.
  • “this circle of creation, all of one piece having no beginning and no end”: The wedding ring has long stood for eternity. It is worn on the fourth finger, where an old belief placed a vein running to the heart.
  • “a handful of rice or confetti or white rose petals”: Rice was thrown for fertility, a bride wore “something old” such as her mother’s veil, and the bride who caught the bouquet would be the next to marry.
  • “to carry her across the threshold”: The custom goes back to Rome. A bride who stumbled at the door brought bad luck, and Madge “had stumbled on her way to the altar.”
  • “the Justice of the Peace to tie the knot”: A justice of the peace could perform a civil marriage without a church or guests.
  • “love, honor, and obey”: The older prayer book vows had only the bride promise to “obey.” Madge throws the word at Homer.
  • “She carried the yellow tuberoses at the commencement”: Tuberoses, heavily fragrant, were favorite flowers at Victorian funerals.
  • “Death comes to every wedding feast”: In Holbein’s Dance of Death (1538) a skeleton drums ahead of a newly married couple.

Chapter 7 · The Graveyard

  • A place of refuge and sustenance for Musidora and her children, representing the blurred line between life and death. One of the last public places where people can gather.

Chapter 8 · The Graveyard Hill

  • Represents the boundary between life and death, a literal and figurative crossroads on the journey.

Chapter 8 · Names on Tombstones

  • Names like Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, and others evoke lineage, memory, and the passage of generations, underscoring the permanence of death. Longtree is Esther’s last name, a character at the end of the novel.

Chapter 9 · Marriage and Reproduction Imagery

  • Miss MacIntosh’s lectures on marriage, ovaries, and reproduction are laden with symbolic meaning about societal expectations, femininity, and the passage into adulthood.
  • The metaphor of flowers needing a man to be impregnated (not just wind) symbolizes the necessity of union and procreation in life, reflecting the cultural norms around marriage and gender roles.

Chapter 10 · Wedding/Funeral Ceremony

  • Symbolizes the intertwined nature of beginnings and endings, union and separation.

Chapter 10

  • “pots and pans jangling in my ears”: A shivaree, or charivari, was the old custom of banging pots and pans outside newlyweds’ windows on their wedding night.
  • “we are gathered here in the sight of God and of this company to join man and woman together”: The Book of Common Prayer opens the marriage service, “Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation, to join together this man and this woman in holy matrimony.”
  • “Do either of ye know of an impediment to this marriage”: The phrase is from the Book of Common Prayer, which drew on the Sarum rite. It reads, “I require and charge you both, as ye will answer at the dreadful day of judgment when the secrets of all hearts shall be disclosed, that if either of you know any impediment . . . ye do now confess it,” and calls on anyone who knows a cause to “speak, or else hereafter for ever hold his peace.”
  • “Unadvisedly or lightly, marriage should not be entered in”: The prayer book says marriage is “not by any to be enterprised, nor taken in hand, unadvisedly, lightly . . . but reverently, discreetly, advisedly, soberly.”
  • “the rites for the burial of the dead”: Funeral rites originated from Jewish and Roman customs. The Order for the Burial of the Dead in the Book of Common Prayer is the service the preacher slides into.
  • “the turtle Solomon and the red geranium and an old, empty shoe”: An old shoe was thrown after the bride or tied to the carriage for luck.

Chapter 14 · The Funeral and the Graveyard

  • The funeral scenes, especially Mr. Spitzer’s brother’s funeral, symbolize mourning, loss, and the passage of time.
  • Catherine’s absence from funerals and the details of the mourning rituals emphasize her detachment and the fragmented nature of her existence.

Chapter 14

  • “the funeral gondola with the corrugated angel at its helm”: Venice carries its dead by black gondola to the cemetery island of San Michele. Liszt wrote “La lugubre gondola” (1882) foreseeing Wagner’s death in Venice, and Wagner’s body left by gondola in 1883.

Chapter 15

  • “is always the bridegroom”: The old image of Death and the Maiden, set to music by Schubert.
  • “wedlock is padlock”: From John Ray’s English Proverbs (1670).
  • “one should keep one’s eyes open, but after marriage, one should keep them half shut”: Poor Richard: “Keep your eyes wide open before marriage, half shut afterwards” (1738).

Chapter 16

  • “the black funeral gondola”: Venice’s black funeral gondolas.

Chapter 16 · The House as a Tomb and Water Castle

  • The grand house is described with imagery of tombs, water, and underwater life, creating a sense of mystery and timelessness. The references to the phoenix and musical tomb further emphasize themes of death and rebirth.

Chapter 17

  • “visualizing her with a red, curled mustache, that I had been right in assigning to her the role of the bridegroom”: The red mustache of Chapter 9 and the wedding dream of Chapter 10.

Chapter 18

  • “every heart is married to death who is the bridegroom and the bride”: Death as the bridegroom, as in Chapter 15. It means that human life is fundamentally intertwined with death. Death is not an external threat but a constant, intimate presence in life. It emphasizes the tragic and inevitable nature of mortality that defines and shapes human existence, love, and relationships. This theme is woven throughout the novel, in the narrator’s reflections on life, death, and illusion.
  • “The tallow is burning low. We have no oil.”: The foolish virgins of the parable say, “Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out” (Matthew 25:8), and miss the bridegroom.

Chapter 20

  • “Was she deserted at the altar by her bridegroom or her bride?”: Compare Miss Havisham in Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), jilted on her wedding day, who stopped every clock and wore her wedding dress ever after.

Chapter 21

  • “as when Mr. Spitzer had taken it out of its long white box”: The dress of Chapter 9. Mr. Spitzer promised, “Fair as a bride I should be,” and Miss MacIntosh complained of its low neck and lack of sleeves.

Chapter 32 · Death as a Wedding and Wedding as Death

  • The narrative blurs the boundaries between life milestones and death: “weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings”. This imagery underscores the theme of transformation and loss inherent in marriage and life.
  • Catherine’s vague, elusive descriptions of her marriage (to a phantom, a porpoise, a star, an iceberg) symbolize the illusory or absent nature of her union and love. Marriage here is a symbolic death of the self or an eternal separation, while death is the final union.

  • The multiple, shifting bridegrooms (white camel, church steeple, wind) reflect the fluidity of identity and reality.

  • Represents grandeur, loss, and the blending of significant life events into one confusing memory.

Chapter 42 · The Bridegroom and Withered Flowers

  • Represent unfulfilled love and abandonment, contrasting with Cousin Hannah’s militant independence and loneliness.
