  • Symbolizes unresolved debts, both literal and metaphorical. The suit represents Peron’s dignity and the past that Mr. Spitzer attempts to honor and settle.

  • A place associated with both death and life, symbolizing the cycle of existence and the blurred line between endings and beginnings.

Definition from research

Chapter 15

Listed as: The old, blind sheep dog

  • The sheep dog’s barking is repeatedly mentioned as an ominous sign, something that "had not barked for nothing," unlike a young dog who barks merely for pleasure. This suggests that the dog's barking is a deliberate warning of danger lurking nearby, perhaps a threat to Vera's innocence or safety.
  • Miss MacIntosh explicitly warns Vera to be careful because "someone who would take a young girl by the hair and drag her into the shadows where her cries should not be heard" might be near.
  • The dog’s barking seems to symbolize a protective instinct, alerting to the presence of real dangers in the night that Vera might be tempted to ignore or not fully understand.
  • The dog is described as "old" and "blind," which adds complexity to its symbolism. Blindness here can be interpreted as a metaphor for the limitations of perception that come with age or experience.
  • While the dog cannot see, it still hears and senses danger, which may suggest that wisdom or vigilance does not solely depend on sight or youthful alertness.
  • The dog’s blindness could also represent the older generation’s partial understanding of dangers, aware but not fully able to prevent them. This aligns with Vera’s reflections on how older people, including Miss MacIntosh, fail to grasp the "heart of youth" and the deeper currents of life and death.
  • The dog’s old age and blindness also evoke mortality and the approach of death, consistent with the chapter’s pervasive meditation on death as a "bridegroom" and the many faces of death.
  • The old blind sheep dog is isolated in the night, barking at waves and wind, much like Vera’s own sense of separation from the older generation and their "adult fantasies."
  • On a narrative level, the dog's barking serves as a tension-building device. It punctuates the chapter’s meditative and philosophical tone with a concrete, audible signal of danger. It brings the abstract themes of death, danger, and innocence into a tangible presence, grounding Vera's lofty reflections in the physical reality of the night and the environment.
  • “The old sheep dog barking in the night had not barked for nothing”: The proverb is “An old dog barks not in vain,” from George Herbert’s Outlandish Proverbs (1640).

Chapter 18

  • The old blind sheep dog appears only briefly and indirectly. It may function as a potent symbol of failing protection, limited perception, and the human struggle to confront elusive and overwhelming existential truths. Its presence underscores the chapter’s meditation on vulnerability, loss, and the elusive nature of reality and memory.
  • Vera hears him barking “perhaps at a spar, perhaps at the last falling star… or some danger greater than any I could have imagined.”

It encapsulates a meditation on missed warnings, silent tragedies, and the profound isolation felt by characters like Vera and Miss MacIntosh as they navigate a world filled with unseen dangers and unspoken sorrows.

lucie-bell:
Lucie Bell

Home

In the research: Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 82

  • She appears as a complex and symbolic figure intertwined deeply with themes of love, silence, and loss. She is depicted not merely as a character but almost as an embodiment of elusive and silent love within a world fraught with communication barriers and existential solitude. Lucie Bell is portrayed as a "silent girl" who is intimately connected to silence and absence of speech. The narrator, Vera, hears a man's voice repeatedly calling out to her, lamenting that Lucie Bell be "a little bird girl with such a small, pecking face and such long, thin legs" who "make[s] too much noise" and is "not my love" because she cannot answer him or give love in return through words. This man’s voice speaks of a deep yearning for a silent love, one that transcends verbal communication, which reflects the novel’s broader preoccupation with the limits and possibilities of communication. Lucie Bell represents a love that exists beyond spoken language, a theme emphasized by the stone-deaf man's narrative. He explains how he hears not with ears but with his eyes and fingers, experiencing the world through a different sensory reality. Lucie Bell’s silence and absence echo the deaf man’s experience, symbolizing a love that must be understood through nonverbal means, through "the tongues of silence speaking the name of love". Her silence is not emptiness but a different form of communication and connection, one that is accessible only through deep empathy or alternative perception. The man who calls out to her also expresses feelings of abandonment and unfaithfulness, suggesting that Lucie Bell left him or was "fickle," loving a jukebox or a "tired marathon skater" more than him. This reflects a tension between presence and absence, fidelity and loss, which permeates the narrative. Lucie Bell’s departure before Vera arrives adds to the sense of missed connections and unfulfilled love in the novel. Although Vera never sees or hears Lucie Bell directly, she deeply loves the deaf man who loved Lucie Bell, indicating that Lucie Bell serves as a bridge or catalyst for Vera’s understanding of love in a silent, fragmented world. Lucie Bell’s absence and silence foreground Vera’s own quest for connection amidst loss and the failure of conventional communication. Lucie Bell can be seen as part of the novel’s meditation on sensory loss, altered perception, and the mysteries of human connection. Just as the narrator reflects on the deafness, blindness, and the nature of communication beyond the ear and eye, Lucie Bell embodies the challenge of loving and being loved when traditional modes of interaction fail or are absent.

  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed as fiercely grounded in what she calls “common sense,” valuing the “middle brow,” the “middle way,” and the “average life,” a disposition she prides herself on as her “greatest love,” even if others despise it.
  • This common sense coexists with a pervasive skepticism toward accepted truths such as history, geography, and law, which she dismisses as unstable, uncertain, or outright falsehoods.
  • She challenges grand narratives, like that of Caesar crossing the Rubicon or the veracity of historical figures, suggesting that time has neither accumulated nor taught wisdom.
  • This skeptical realism reveals a character who questions the foundations of knowledge and human pretensions but does so without despair; rather, she seems to accept human limitations with a certain weary humor and irony.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s discourse centers on her criticism of modern inventions, especially electric lights. She associates electricity, notably Benjamin Franklin’s experiments, as a disruptive force that has destroyed natural rhythms, privacy, and the quietness of night. She laments electric lights for erasing darkness, which she sees as essential for sleep, privacy, and even mystery in human relationships, particularly marriage. Electric lights, she argues, expose flaws and imperfections that were once safely hidden in darkness, thereby damaging marriages and social harmony.
  • Her detailed critique extends to “electric trains,” “electric irons,” “fluorescent lamps,” and “two-way lighting systems” as unnatural intrusions into life’s natural order.
  • This stance encapsulates her resistance to tampering with “old, damaged creation” and her preference for simpler, older ways such as “bayberry candles,” “snuffers,” and natural starlight. Her view is that the modern world’s brightness is a form of extravagant excess that impoverishes human experience and dignity.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s practical nature is emphasized by descriptions of her appearance and habits. She dresses plainly, in worn, practical clothing: a grey baseball sweater with a ravelling sleeve, stout shoes, and a patched salt-and-pepper tweed coat.
  • She carries her “rigging” everywhere, including an old black umbrella likened to a sail and a whale-boned ice-breaker corset, symbolizing her preparedness and no-nonsense approach to life on a “rough shore.”
  • She rejects frivolities such as filmy dresses or adornments, even on significant occasions like weddings or funerals, signaling her seriousness and focus on the immediate, tangible world rather than on dreams or illusions.
  • Despite her talk of cosmic and remote issues like glaciers, submerged continents, and the first days of creation, Miss MacIntosh reveals little of her personal emotions or vulnerabilities.
  • She claims her consciousness ceases during sleep and that she cannot remember dreams, not even her own, suggesting a detachment from inner emotional life or a guardedness.
  • Her conscience “kept guard” as a “lonely vigil,” indicating solitude and perhaps a self-imposed emotional isolation.
  • She evades personal disclosures and remains impassive, almost austere, in her demeanor.
  • This emotional reserve contrasts with the vastness of the cosmic themes she invokes, highlighting a tension between the grand and the personal.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections often shift from the mundane to the cosmic and from daily life and societal critiques to the “first starfish upon the first beach” and “the first moon drawing the first tide.” This oscillation suggests that she perceives human life as part of a vast, impersonal natural order that transcends immediate existence.
  • She uses cosmic imagery to mask what she does not want to reveal: her fears, losses, or inner life.
  • This duality makes her a somewhat enigmatic figure, connecting the earthly and the universal while remaining personally elusive.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s thoughts about the coming winter, the colorlessness of the world under snow and ice, and the need to prepare with warm clothing and supplies reveal a keen awareness of mortality and the cycles of life.
  • Winter symbolizes death or hardship, and her sober preparation indicates acceptance rather than fear. Yet, she also acknowledges the subtle beauty of winter’s muted colors, reflecting a nuanced appreciation of life’s phases and transitions.
  • Her concern with time’s passing, the loss inherent in change, and the persistence of “dimmed colors” in hardship underscore a mature, grounded philosophy.
  • Throughout her discourse, Miss MacIntosh repeatedly condemns human vanity, illusions of grandeur, and false hopes.
  • She refers to “vain man” in multiple historical and contemporary contexts, from Emperor Constantine and Caesar to Benjamin Franklin, pointing out the futility of human pretensions to immortality or mastery.
  • She warns against illusions, falsehoods that may mask other truths, and the human tendency to stumble blindly in the “broad daylight which God has lighted.”
  • Her repeated invocation of vanity and illusion underscores a theme of human limitation and the importance of humility and realism.

Chapter 1

  • Vera and seeker, deeply introspective and philosophical, haunted by loss and the search for truth.

Chapter 3

  • A child who has escaped from her mother’s “opium paradise.”
  • Looks up to Miss MacIntosh as a guide and protector.
  • Observes and reflects on the strange atmosphere and characters around her.

Chapter 4

  • Deeply affected by Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance or death.
  • Battles between despair, illusions, and the desire for a meaningful life.
  • Struggles with her mother’s (Catherine) perception of her sanity.
  • Embodies themes of mourning, hope, and transformation.

Chapter 5

  • Vera watches the bus-driver and the other passengers, including Madge, capturing their physical and emotional states with a keen, almost clinical eye. She notes Madge's moaning and accusing, Moses's erratic behavior and long hair, and the desolate landscape outside. Her observations are detailed, conveying a sense of decay, confusion, and suspended time.
  • Vera's narration is imbued with philosophical undertones. She reflects on themes of life and death, creation and destruction, reality and illusion.
  • She engages with the bus-driver's thoughts and conversations, especially his long monologue about his hair, politics, and existential musings.
  • Vera seems to understand the symbolic weight of the bus-driver's hair as a metaphor for identity, resistance to corruption, and his connection to life amid death.
  • Vera's narration conveys a sense of uncertainty about the reality of their situation. The bus-driver himself seems caught between dreaming and waking, life and death, and Vera shares this ambiguity.
  • She hints that the bus-driver may be dead or dreaming, trapped in a liminal space where time loops and places vanish. This uncertainty colors her perspective, making her more contemplative and less definitive in her judgments.
  • Vera is empathetic to the people around her. She also maintains a certain detachment. She does not intervene or change the course of events but rather records them with a mixture of sorrow, irony, and resignation. Her tone suggests an understanding of the tragic absurdity of their journey and the existential plight of the characters.
  • Vera functions as a bridge between the reader and the symbolic, almost hallucinatory world of the chapter and for the rest of the novel. Through her narration, the reader gains access to the bus-driver's inner turmoil, the desolate landscape, and the metaphysical questions raised.
  • Vera's bus trip exists in a liminal space between reality and dream, serving as a profound metaphor for her search for life and truth amid the illusions and uncertainties that surround her.

Chapter 8

  • Her descriptions are richly metaphorical and poetic, often blending natural imagery with existential or mythic overtones.
  • She imparts a sense of transition or passage not just through physical space but through states of being or time.
  • She frequently distances herself from the events, perceiving them as if in a vision or dream.
  • She is grappling with realities that are elusive, fragmented, or overwhelming.
  • She contemplates mortality, memory, and identity. This reflects an engagement with themes of impermanence and the unknowability of ultimate fate.
  • While observing others on the bus, Vera remains somewhat apart, bearing witness to their stories and conflicts without fully participating.
  • Her grief and confusion suggest a loneliness or estrangement, emphasized by the eerie, almost spectral description of the village and its inhabitants.
  • Vera is positioned on the edge of the known and unknown, the living and the dead, the earthly and the eternal.
  • The stopping of the bus at a fork, one path leading to a graveyard hill and the other to a mysterious village of promise, serves as a potent symbol for her liminal condition. This reflects an internal or spiritual threshold, not merely a physical one.
  • Her tone is somber, contemplative, and at times skeptical or cynical, especially in the bus-driver’s monologue on medical science, mortality, and social decay. She absorbs this skepticism without endorsing it outright, contributing to a complex, layered narrative voice.

Chapter 9

  • A young girl on the cusp of adolescence, navigating strict domestic training and her own inner dreams.
  • Exhibits a tension between obedience and rebellion.
  • Yearns for love, adventure, and a meaningful future beyond the mundane expectations set by Miss MacIntosh.
  • Reflects deeply on identity, mortality, and the mystery of human relationships.

Chapter 10

Chapter 11

  • Reflects on isolation and the difficulty of enduring it without resorting to illusions.

Chapter 12

  • Reflective, imaginative, and sensitive.
  • Struggles between embracing imagination and dreams and confronting reality.
  • Experiences moments of joy and freedom but also faces the harsh truths of life and mortality.
  • At seven she bayed like a dog, dug for bones, heard the dead, and believed she was Chopin reborn, until Miss MacIntosh “restored me to my senses.”

Chapter 13

  • She begins with a poignant farewell to the "last certitude," including the tender moment of her fourteenth birthday and the figure of Miss MacIntosh, who had been a constant presence for seven years.
  • This farewell symbolizes a significant psychological and emotional shift: a departure from innocence and an acknowledgement that the familiar is no longer certain or reliable.
  • Vera admits to having taken Miss MacIntosh for granted, thinking her the most ordinary person, only to realize she was mysterious and unknowable. This signals an awakening to the complexity and ambiguity of human beings and relationships.
  • She compares her previous ignorance to a weary traveler crossing a frozen lake under unbearable conditions, unaware that the ice beneath is treacherous and that survival was against all odds.
  • This metaphor vividly captures the precariousness of Vera’s former worldview: one that was sheltered and unknowing, yet preserved her from the shock of truth.
  • The crossing into awareness is described as a moment of death and rebirth, forever altering perception: "Everything... would be different... the simplest gesture having a different meaning".
  • Following this awakening, Vera experiences a profound fragmentation of reality, where the familiar world loses its coherence and reliability.
  • The surrounding environment, including natural elements like moons, stars, and waters, fails to provide reassurance.
  • Vera explicitly bids farewell to “old moralities,” “proverbial wisdom,” and “the past and its illusion,” highlighting a rejection of previously accepted truths and a plunge into existential uncertainty.
  • Her farewell to the past is not simple nostalgia but a confrontation with the past as a “dream” that must be “laid bare like a corpse.”
  • This suggests a critical and almost forensic examination of memory, recognizing that the past is layered with deception as well as unexpected truths. Vera anticipates surprise and shock in discovering the absence of qualities once assumed and the presence of others previously unrecognized.
  • Vera’s reflections are imbued with elaborate, poetic imagery. These images evoke a dreamlike, liminal space between reality and illusion, life and death, sound and silence.
  • The “garden of the deaf,” where “the ear is dead,” becomes a powerful symbol of isolation, silence, and possibly the failure or refusal of communication.
  • Her environment is suffused with paradox and ambiguity, reflecting Vera’s inner turmoil and the collapse of conventional understanding.
  • Vera wrestles with themes of presence and absence, sound and silence, life and death.
  • Throughout the chapter, Vera’s tone is melancholic, marked by a sense of loss, estrangement, and an almost mournful awareness of change.
  • The farewell to Miss MacIntosh and the past, the dissection of memory, and the surreal descriptions of the garden convey a profound alienation from the world once known, both external and internal.

  • Experiences a physical and psychological battle with the transformed Miss MacIntosh.
  • Reflects on memories, identity, and the nature of illusion versus reality.

Chapter 18

Chapter 19

  • She describes her mind as “lucid as day” but simultaneously reveals a hesitation or reluctance to fully open her eyes and confront reality directly. This tension between clarity and avoidance suggests an internal conflict or a fragile psychological state. She seems caught between the realms of dream and waking, reality and imagination, as shown by her uncertainty about whether she is truly awake despite the vividness of the dawn light and surroundings.
  • She meticulously catalogues the objects and conditions in Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom, from the “crumbling heads of cherubim” to the “red wig, almost purple,” and the “jeweled water glass” holding false teeth. This detailed observation indicates a careful, almost forensic attention to detail, suggesting a mind that seeks to understand and piece together the significance of the environment and the person within it.
  • There is a tone of gentle curiosity in Vera’s internal questioning about Miss MacIntosh’s peculiarities: her missing eyebrows, the changing colors of her skin, her habitual wearing of hats and a whistle, and the careful way she avoids showing vulnerability (the umbrella carried “like a shield uplifted where there was no gale”). These questions are posed with “studied detachment,” as if Vera is trying to maintain emotional distance while simultaneously probing deeply into the character of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Despite this detachment, Vera’s sensitivity is apparent in her awareness of the “quiver of wind upon the high cheek bones,” the “thin, ascetic mouth,” and the “wet and stained” pillow. She notices intimate, tender details such as the fact that “one breast had been amputated,” describing what remains as “no bigger than a baby’s,” which evokes a sense of vulnerability and loss. This reveals an underlying empathy and a recognition of Miss MacIntosh’s suffering and resilience.
  • Vera recalls Miss MacIntosh’s sayings that “the Devil’s cards are marked” and that she “knew not… of these dualities in one heart, these double motions.”
  • Vera’s detailed description of Miss MacIntosh’s room (with its broken, bare, and patched furnishings, barred door, and scattered personal effects) reflects a broader sense of isolation, hardship, and complexity. She seems attuned to this atmosphere of loneliness and endurance, which may mirror her own inner state or the broader themes of the narrative.

Chapter 66

  • Vera is deeply influenced by Miss MacIntosh, to the point of reflecting her moods and taking on "every color except my own". This suggests a lack of a strong, independent identity in her childhood, making her highly susceptible to Miss MacIntosh's unusual worldview.
  • Vera is often confused by Miss MacIntosh's lessons and pronouncements. She admits to being "very stupid, undeveloped" and unable to answer basic questions. However, this also implies a certain level of intellectual curiosity, even if she struggles to grasp the concepts.
  • As a child, Vera takes Miss MacIntosh's eccentricities for granted, considering them "commonplace". This acceptance highlights her innocence and the way children often normalize the unusual behavior of adults in their lives.
  • The narrative is framed as a recollection from "long years after Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance". This distance allows Vera to view the lessons with "a new light," recognizing their unorthodox nature. The nostalgic tone suggests that Miss MacIntosh, despite her strangeness, had a significant impact on Vera's life and development.
  • Vera seems haunted by Miss MacIntosh's disappearance and the circumstances surrounding it. The recurring imagery of storms, drowning, and the sea suggests a deep sense of loss and unresolved questions. She can still hear Miss MacIntosh's voice "roaring above the storm" 829, indicating a lasting psychological impact.
  • Vera's observation that Miss MacIntosh wished to tell her all her secrets during the last month of her life suggests a growing awareness and understanding of her nursemaid's complexities. She begins to perceive Miss MacIntosh's loneliness, her longing for adult companionship, and her hidden vulnerabilities, such as her baldness.
  • Even as a child, Vera seems to possess a keen eye for the absurd. She notices the incongruities in Miss MacIntosh's behavior, such as her wearing a whaler's hat during lessons or receiving an Eskimo cookbook as a gift when she never cooks. This suggests an underlying sense of humor and an ability to recognize the strangeness of the world around her.
  • In retrospect, Vera reflects on her own shortcomings and tendencies, such as her proneness to hallucinations and her lack of a distinct identity. This introspection suggests a desire to understand herself and her relationship with Miss MacIntosh on a deeper level.

Chapter 70

  • Vera emerges as a deeply introspective, highly imaginative, and somewhat detached individual whose internal world often blurs with external reality. Her character is defined by a profound engagement with dreams, a complex relationship with her past, and a unique way of perceiving and constructing reality.
  • She explicitly states that Mrs. Hogden, a central figure in this chapter, is someone she "never saw", but rather a "trick of my imagination, this substituting of the one for the other". Vera acknowledges Mrs. Hogden as a "substitute... for the dream life I wanted" and even calls her "my mind’s betrayal of my mind". This self-awareness about her mental constructs highlights her active internal world, where figures like Mrs. Hogden go “waddling in and out of my dreams.” She can "see" Mrs. Hogden by simply "closing my eyes, by concentrating". This constant blurring of waking life, dreams, and imaginative constructs suggests that Vera's consciousness is the primary lens through which the narrative unfolds, making her a subjective and unreliable, yet compelling, narrator.
  • Vera's character is also deeply shaped by her past and the figures who influenced her upbringing, particularly Miss MacIntosh and her mother. Miss MacIntosh, Vera's former nursemaid, "brought me up to understand that my mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman such as she saw me becoming, a woman like herself, simple and average and clear-eyed". This suggests that Miss MacIntosh tried to instill a sense of conventionality in Vera, despite Vera's inherent imaginative tendencies (Miss MacIntosh "would have disapproved of, most ardently" of night-dreaming). Vera's "escaped from my mother’s house" further indicates a strained relationship with her mother, who is portrayed as eccentric and prone to "frenzied dreaming". Vera's ongoing comparison of Mrs. Hogden to Miss MacIntosh, even after Miss MacIntosh's death, shows her lingering attachment to these formative figures and her effort to understand her own identity through their contrasting influences.
  • Despite her imaginative immersion, Vera demonstrates a keen observational and analytical mind, though often applied to her internal world. She meticulously describes Mrs. Hogden's outlandish appearance and actions, down to the "smashed hat with a wilted ostrich feather" and the "row of Javanese temple bells". She also notices the "evidence left by Mrs. Hogden" in the playroom, such as "derelict whiskey bottles, empty coat hangers, withered apple cores, broken egg shells, dead flies", distinguishing even an "artificial eyelash". Her philosophical reflections, such as her belief in a "small, warped flower growing... outside the consciousness of God", reveal a mind that questions universal truths and finds significance in anomalies.
  • Vera also conveys a sense of loneliness and a search for meaning or connection. She explicitly states, "The life I required was the life which required, like his, a lost companion —not merely this self-centered affliction of the right hand loving the left". Her observation that "Everybody is lonely" suggests a deep, shared human experience she identifies with. Mrs. Hogden, as an imagined companion, could be seen as Vera's attempt to fill this void, even while acknowledging the illusion
  • Vera's identity appears somewhat fluid and permeable. Mrs. Hogden mistakenly supposes Vera to be Lisa Lunde, and Vera herself often blurs the lines between her own experiences, her mother's dreams, and the fabricated reality of Mrs. Hogden. This fluidity contributes to the dreamlike atmosphere of the chapter and underscores Vera's role as a narrator whose self is not rigidly defined, but rather an evolving construct shaped by memory, imagination, and the enigmatic characters she encounters, both real and imagined.

Chapter 71

  • An observer and participant, reflecting on the surreal and tragic elements of the setting.
  • Vera, the narrator, emerges as a deeply contemplative and psychologically complex figure, marked by a blend of wakefulness, memory, and a searching, somewhat haunted awareness.
  • Vera is awake in the cold, grey morning, unable or unwilling to sleep despite the silence and stillness around her. Her state is described as "stiff with wakefulness, with ceaseless memory" and "wide awake, alert, watchful," showing a restless mind that is both physically and mentally active rather than at rest. This wakefulness seems not merely physical but also symbolic, representing a state of consciousness probing the mysteries and uncertainties of her surroundings and her own psyche.
  • Throughout the chapter, Vera’s thoughts drift into rich, imaginative flights and reflections. She muses on the Christian hangman and his tragic personal history, pondering whether he might hang himself or wait for dawn because of his children playing at hanging themselves. These ruminations blend reality with dreamlike speculation, demonstrating her tendency to think metaphorically and symbolically. Vera also reflects on her mother’s pearls, linking them to ideas of loss, infinity, and the elusive nature of reality and memory.
  • Vera is portrayed as a traveler or outsider in this strange, desolate Indiana hotel and its surroundings. She is "some time past the ambiguity of dawn," wearing travel-stained clothes and carrying her mother’s lace and pearls, symbols of a "lost estate" and an unrealized past. Her presence in the hotel is that of someone searching for something: wild flowers of spring, beauty, or perhaps a deeper meaning amid the decay and disorder around her. This sense of quest is tinged with uncertainty and disillusionment, as the landscape and people she encounters are far removed from her expectations or hopes.
  • Vera is a keen observer of the strange and unsettling characters she encounters, especially the doctor, Dr. O’Leary, and the hangman. She notes the doctor’s madness and the surreal disorder of his office and life, filled with instruments, scattered shoes of various types and eras, and imaginary patients. Vera reflects on the blending of reality and fantasy, the doctor’s second childhood, and the presence of "imaginary babies" and a "pregnant man," indicating her awareness of the blurred lines between sanity and madness, reality and hallucination.
  • Vera listens to the angry widow who confronts her, accusing her of being a "tramp girl" who kept her awake all night, and to Tabitha, the muted chambermaid who quietly carries out her duties. Despite these confrontations and the vivid descriptions of the inhabitants’ misery and anger, Vera seems somewhat detached as an intruder or observer rather than a participant. She tries to explain herself logically but acknowledges the complexity and strangeness of the place and its people.
  • Vera’s narrative voice often becomes poetic and philosophical, contemplating themes of time, memory, loss, and the impermanence of life. She notes how the hotel room expands during sleeplessness into a vast landscape of memory and future, blending space and time. Her thoughts on the pearls, on the dreamlike quality of the world, and on the symbolic meaning of the doctor's books and instruments show a mind attuned to deeper existential questions.
  • Vera is a searching, sensitive, and somewhat alienated narrator, caught between wakefulness and dreams, reality and fantasy, memory and the present. Her observations are rich with symbolism and emotional depth, portraying her as a figure grappling with the mysteries of life, madness, and the passage of time in a world that is both concrete and surreal.

  • The contrast between her vitality and the decay and ruin described elsewhere in the chapter highlights the fragility of life and the relentless passage of time.
  • Jacqueline represents a fleeting glimpse of beauty and life amidst a landscape marked by death, desolation, and resignation.

Definition from research

Chapter 70

  • Lisa Lunde is introduced as Vera's mother's "young companion who took my place when, carrying a large suitcase, I escaped from my mother’s house". This immediately establishes her as a replacement for Vera and suggests a practical, perhaps less privileged, background. Indeed, she is described as a "would-be physicist working for her living in order to help support her mother who was poor and mad and dreamed that she was rich", highlighting her sense of responsibility and pragmatic drive, contrasting with the opulence and delusion of Vera's mother's household.
  • Lisa Lunde is characterized by her analytical, skeptical, and often blunt nature. She "prided herself on seeing immediately through Mrs. Hogden’s pretensions" and quickly assesses Mrs. Hogden as a "very dubious character, a shoplifter or something equally vicious". Definition from research

Chapter 73

Listed as: The Chicago detective

  • A symbolic figure representing societal judgment, scrutiny, and the external pressures faced by Esther Longtree. Though he appears only indirectly through Esther’s thoughts and fears, his presence is significant and multifaceted.
  • The detective symbolizes the potential legal and moral condemnation that Esther fears. She imagines a scenario where she might be arrested, tried, and accused of murder for the stillborn children she has carried and lost over the years. The detective’s investigation represents society’s attempt to impose order and assign blame on Esther for the tragic outcomes of her pregnancies, despite her innocence in her own mind.
  • The detective is described as "old" and "sterile," highlighting a contrast with Esther’s "everlasting pregnancy." He stands for the many fathers who impregnated Esther but who were unable or unwilling to assume responsibility for the children, especially since most of the children were stillborn or never fully born. The detective’s search for proof and evidence reflects a broader theme of male absence and desertion, with Esther bearing the burden alone.
  • Esther fears the detective’s inquiries, which might lead to public exposure of her condition and the stillborn children. She worries about appearing before a jury while visibly pregnant, the social humiliation involved, and the invasive nature of such an investigation. This fear adds to her isolation and suffering, emphasizing the harshness of societal judgment towards women in her position.
  • The detective’s efforts to find evidence of murder or wrongdoing are ultimately futile, as Esther has hidden the stillborn children in natural places (streams, fields, under snowdrifts) making proof elusive. This futility underscores the theme of invisibility and loss that permeates Esther’s life and the narrative. The detective’s inability to find tangible evidence mirrors Esther’s own uncertainty about the fate and existence of the children.
  • Through the detective’s imagined role, the narrator Vera explores themes of justice, mercy, and the limits of human understanding. Esther’s silence and refusal to answer inquiries, partly motivated by kindness to the dying fathers and partly by self-preservation, contrast with the detective’s probing. This tension raises questions about who is truly culpable and how society deals with grief and loss.

  • He is investigating murders but is ironically implicated in Esther’s personal tragedy through his actions.

In the research: Chapter 80

Definition from research

Chapter 80

  • Walter is a profoundly complex and symbolic character. He is Esther Longtree's first-born child, a figure who embodies both literal and metaphorical dimensions of life, death, guilt, and memory.
  • Walter is described as a child whom Esther had "killed," yet paradoxically, he "lived." This duality makes him a ghostly presence; both alive and dead in the narrative reality. Esther hears his cries, feels his accusations, and wrestles with the burden of her guilt and regret that he represents. Walter's persistent questioning, “Mother, why have you killed me?” and “Where is my father?”, haunts Esther’s conscience, embodying her unatoned sin and unresolved emotional pain.
  • Walter acts as a relentless accuser who confronts Esther with her past actions and their consequences. His presence "keeps her working," making her scrub floors and endure long hours in the restaurant. He embodies the emotional and psychological torment that Esther cannot escape. His accusations are unanswerable, and he seems to have a cruel, hard heart, adding to Esther’s suffering.
  • Walter is portrayed with specific physical features, "black as my true love, black as my heart", reflecting his mixed racial heritage, which complicates Esther’s feelings toward him. His blackness symbolizes difference and alienation, as well as the social challenges unresolved in Esther's life. The fact that his father was black and a "prince of Africa" adds layers to Walter’s identity, evoking themes of race, social stigma, and forbidden love.
  • Walter represents the "beloved obstacle" to Esther’s life and future. His existence and the guilt attached to him prevent her from fully embracing motherhood and happiness. Esther’s many stillborn children and miscarriages contrast with Walter’s unique status as the one child who lived but remained emotionally inaccessible. Walter is both the cause of her endless pregnancies and the reason for her emotional isolation.
  • Walter is inseparable from Esther’s memories, a persistent shadow in her mind. He symbolizes a trauma that has not been resolved: her fear, shame, and the consequences of a youthful mistake. The narrator, Vera, reveals that Walter's presence is intertwined with Esther’s perception of time, reality, and self, blurring lines between life and death, memory and present.
  • Walter is central to the chapter’s meditation on birth, death, life’s incompleteness, and the mysteries of existence. Esther’s dialogue with Walter, his questioning, and his haunting presence articulate the theme that life is an ongoing negotiation between presence and absence, love and loss, guilt and redemption.
  • Walter is not merely a character but a symbolic force representing Esther’s guilt, lost motherhood, racial complexity, and the unresolved past that haunts her. He is a living accusation and a ghostly memory, a child who should have died but has instead become an eternal presence in Esther’s life, shaping her identity and destiny.

  • The recurring motif of the "dead ear," especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer and Catherine, underscores a world where communication fails and the essence of existence is isolated from meaning.
  • Catherine’s insistence that "the ear was dead" and that "there was not a sound to be heard" suggests a bleak vision of human experience as disembodied from relational and sensory engagement.

  • Catherine’s fear of the silence "unbroken by the sound" and her particular dread "when a frog screamed" indicate deep psychological distress. The silence is oppressive, a void that she cannot endure, and the rare disruptive sounds become sources of terror rather than comfort. This paradox of fearing both silence and sudden noise points to a troubled mind caught between extremes, fragile and haunted.

Listed as: Catherine (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine is described as bedridden, veiled in white lace and surrounded by an atmosphere of drifting snowflakes, candle flames, and reflections. She is physically confined and vulnerable, a "creature of such fragility" who is easily overwhelmed by the presence of Cousin Hannah and the harshness of reality. Her bed is a "floating swan bed in a dazzling cloud," which evokes both fragility and an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality. This imagery underscores her physical and emotional weakness.
  • Catherine’s essential loneliness and isolation is emphasized. She is abandoned by the "mysterious bridegroom” and all her loves are imaginary: pharaohs, captains, and other ethereal figures who "had left her, and they had never been". This abandonment extends to emotional desolation, as no one, "not even Cousin Hannah," has ever truly touched her "cold heart," which is "cold and hard as the mountain rock". This coldness suggests an emotional deadness or protective numbness born from pain.
  • Catherine lives largely in a world of dreams, illusions, and shifting realities. She imagines weddings to phantoms, sailboats, stars, and icebergs, reflecting a detachment from conventional life and relationships. Her marriage is portrayed as an ambiguous event, possibly symbolic or imaginary, rather than a concrete historical fact. The wedding imagery ("blushing behind her billowing wedding veils," "married to a phantom") conveys a sense of being caught between life and death, reality and fantasy.
  • Catherine's mental state is described as "changeful and capricious," with a wandering attention and vague memories. She is inconsistent in her accounts and perceptions, which may be interpreted as a symptom of her illness, age, or psychological state. This instability contrasts strongly with Cousin Hannah’s forceful and direct manner, highlighting Catherine’s passivity and internal turmoil.
  • Catherine’s relationship with Cousin Hannah reveals much about her character. Hannah is vigorous, militant, and confrontational, while Catherine simulates emotions she does not feel and "dissembles her feelings" when Hannah visits. Catherine’s indifference masks inner panic and vulnerability. Whereas Hannah is a symbol of active struggle and outward battle, Catherine is an embodiment of internal retreat and quiet suffering. Yet, Catherine admires Hannah’s energy and persistence, even as she is overshadowed by it.
  • Catherine is associated with death-like sleep and a liminal state between life and death. The novel suggests that she is "already dead" in a metaphorical sense, living in a "pretense of death". Her life is marked by a profound stasis, and she may be seen as a "sleeping lady" awaiting awakening or final rest. The imagery of snow, cold, and fading light reinforces this theme of suspended animation and the passage between worlds.
  • Catherine’s marriage and attitude toward men are ambiguous. She married "that great traveller who never would return," possibly to defy Cousin Hannah’s militant feminism or to assert independence, but the marriage was doomed. Her symbolic wedding to various natural and mystical entities rather than a man suggests rejection or transcendence of traditional romantic or marital relationships.
  • Catherine is depicted with a strong aesthetic sensibility: her fingers wear jewels that "gleam like northern lights," and her surroundings are rich in poetic symbolism (flutes, harps, snowflakes, candle flames). She is a "beautiful femme fatale," but her beauty is cold and distant, more a vision than a presence. This artistic and ethereal quality adds to her complexity as a character who inhabits a realm between reality and dream.

Chapter 70

  • Catherine, Vera's mother, is a profoundly eccentric, wealthy invalid whose grasp on reality is tenuous and fragmented. Her character is defined by a series of contradictions, delusions, and a self-centered, often manipulative, approach to those around her.
  • Initially, Vera establishes Catherine as an unconventional figure, noting that Miss MacIntosh, Vera's former nursemaid, raised Vera to understand that her "mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman". Catherine is also revealed as the "true subject of [Vera's] dreams," indicating her deep, almost obsessive, significance to Vera.
  • Catherine's disconnection from reality is a dominant trait. She "dreamed that she was poor," contrasting with Lisa Lunde's mother who "dreamed that she was rich". Her physical and mental state is described as one of profound invalidism, often sinking into "deeper and deeper coma" and experiencing hallucinations, such as "a huge toad was eating my mother’s face" or "the balloon fish floating over my mother’s head", and "shadowy figures stepped out of the walls. There were moths with human faces". She herself admits to having "lost my mind several times" and declares, "I am not responsible for my actions". Her identity is fluid; she believes she has "killed her former self and that my mother’s former self was walking through the house while my mother lay with her hair streaked out like twilight on a pillow, for my mother was dead—added, subtracted, multiplied, divided".
  • Despite her profound mental disarray, Catherine exhibits moments of surprising shrewdness and practicality, particularly concerning financial matters. She can display a "shrewd gleam in her eyes, the absolute efficiency with which she inquired into her financial concerns, past and present," even seeking to collect "Old loans which she had forgotten making" from dead parties. Her instruction to meticulously inspect the house for missing items after Mrs. Hogden's departure further underscores this trait.
  • Catherine's interactions with Mrs. Hogden, her newly arrived companion, highlight her manipulative and self-centered nature. Initially, she feigns "profound, glazed astonishment," denying any knowledge of Mrs. Hogden or having sent an invitation, calling her an "impostor, a liar, a day-dreamer, a thief". Despite Mrs. Hogden possessing intimate details of Catherine's life like "the head of Alcibiades was in the drainpipe" or "a whale swimming into my mother’s bedroom" which only Catherine could have divulged, Catherine still refuses to see her. She employs elaborate excuses, claiming to be "gone to Boston to see a podiatrist" or "to the North Pole". She blames Lisa Lunde for Mrs. Hogden's presence and attempts to discourage Mrs. Hogden by assigning her an uncomfortable "deserted playroom" and a "hospital cot" that was "too short and too narrow". Her ultimate directive to Mr. Spitzer to "push her off a high building or throw her into the ocean" to get rid of Mrs. Hogden reveals a cruel and extreme impulse.
  • Catherine's desire for an arithmetic teacher who would teach "Two and two always making four...over and over again" suggests a yearning for simple, undeniable truths in a chaotic personal reality. However, she rejects Mrs. Hogden's attempts to teach, deeming her "mad as a loon" for repeating the lesson. She views Mrs. Hogden as a "rival invalid" and a "gross, stinking parody" of her own "distended world of shimmering, loosely woven textures", indicating a fierce protectiveness over her unique inner world.
  • Catherine's memory and awareness fluctuate. After Mrs. Hogden's departure, she is "disappointed now that she had not been taught arithmetic and blamed Lisa Lunde", even considering hiring another "lonely old woman" to teach her. This cyclical nature underscores her persistent detachment from the consequences of her actions and her inability to learn from past experiences.

Chapter 71

  • Catherine is a figure deeply immersed in a subjective, dream-like reality, detached from the conventional world. Her character is defined by her peculiar philosophies, eccentric habits, and a luxurious but illusory existence that profoundly shapes Vera's own journey and desires.
  • Catherine is often referred to by Vera as "my sleeping mother", suggesting a state of perpetual dreaming or detachment from waking life. Her physical presence is limited; she "had not walked for many years because of the birthmark staining her cheek and because of her fear of the wavering floor, the sea sweeping in, and her dead past". This immobility further anchors her to her internal world, within her great, "sea-blackened house with gold towers and cornices", which, despite its grandeur, is described as being "gone", implying its existence is more in memory or illusion than current reality.
  • Her unique philosophical outlook is evident in her beliefs about her "real pearls," which, she claimed, "could not be lost or stolen or sold. Whatever the human, unhuman situation might be, those real pearls could not really be lost, and I should wear them, for they were her lost estate". She believed that losing pearls paradoxically led to their multiplication, creating "infinities of pearls," a concept she explained as "just simple arithmetic, simple addition". This belief system defies logic, suggesting a mind that operates on its own fantastical rules. She also held a profound view of existence, stating that it was "probably not... eternity, something everlasting, this being so temporary a world, the world already gone. Only the shadow... ever does come here".
  • Catherine's eccentricity is vividly illustrated through her interaction with a thief who broke into her house one winter night. Far from being alarmed, she "smilingly greeted him, extending her ivory-colored hand, asking him how far he had come, and was the world truly dead, and had offered him drugged sherry". She engaged him in a languorous conversation, "sympathizing with her that she was rich, just as she had sympathized with him that he was poor". In a grand, yet impractical, gesture, she offered to "finance a Revolution" with a blank check, contingent on the thief naming "an exact sum needed and an exact date," which, caught in her "shimmering enchantment," he could not do. Her generosity extended to outfitting the thief in an aristocratic gentleman's costume, including a "high silk opera hat," "long white motor coat," and "white flowers behind his ears," symbolizing the "coming Revolution" and making him "the melting snowman upon the first day of spring". This act demonstrates her theatricality and her desire to transform reality according to her own grand, symbolic visions.
  • Vera carries the tangible and intangible legacy of her mother. She wears Catherine's "black velvet which had been her abandoned shroud," her "lace collar and the lace cuffs," and the "necklace of pearls". These items are not just mementos but symbols of her mother's unique existence and Vera's connection to that past. However, Vera's own desire for "something quite plain and poor and bare" and her search for "order, as if it were a beautiful island in the midst of life" suggest a yearning for a reality distinct from her mother's opulent, yet ultimately vanished, dream-world.   • “Shall love be infinitely postponed? If infinitely postponed, then it is love.” may refer to Hegel. To deny something is to determine it, and to determine something is to negate it. Spinoza’s principle is “every determination is negation”. Hegel takes this one step further by suggesting that negation itself is a process of creation, and is even the essence of positive being. By denying a certain trait or characteristic, one is implicitly acknowledging the possibility of its opposite or the existence of a different reality. For Hegel, this power of the negative, or the act of negation, is what drives progress and development. Denying a particular concept allows for the possibility of a new one to emerge, incorporating both the original concept and its negation. This is often explained through the concept of the negation of the negation, where a denial of a denial leads to a new synthesis that transcends both the original thesis and the antithesis. From an existentialist perspective denying a predefined purpose or essence allows for the possibility of individuals to create their own meaning and existence. The line speaks to love as an infinite emotional state, one that transcends immediate gratification and endures through time, absence, and even death, resonating with the novel's larger themes of longing, loss, and the elusive nature of human connection.

It has its roots in ancient Greek philosophy with Thales and Plato and later with Spinoza, Leibniz, and Schopenhauer. It reflects Mr. Spitzer's profound and troubling awareness of the pervasive presence of consciousness or life-like qualities in all things around him. This means that Mr. Spitzer experiences a kind of existential distress or mental anguish because he perceives consciousness, intention, or awareness not just in people but extending to inanimate objects, natural phenomena, and abstract concepts. He senses life, emotion, or meaning in things that are traditionally considered lifeless, such as clouds, stars, waves, or even shadows and this blurs the line between what is truly alive and what is not. This overwhelming and almost mystical perception causes him suffering because it challenges ordinary reality and makes his own sense of self and understanding of the world unstable and confusing. This agonizing attribution is part of Mr. Spitzer's broader struggle with reality, illusion, memory, and identity. It underlines his sensitivity to the ambiguities and mysteries of existence, where the boundaries between life and death, the living and the non-living, and reality and dream are not distinct. His mind is burdened by this expansive and unsettling sense of interconnectedness and animation of all things, which he cannot easily reconcile or control.   • Peter Abelard was a medieval French scholastic philosopher, leading logician, theologian, teacher, musician, composer, and poet. In Catholic theology, he is best known for his development of the concept of limbo, and his introduction of the moral influence theory of atonement. He is considered (alongside Augustine) to be the most significant forerunner of the modern self-reflective autobiographer. He paved the way and set the tone for later epistolary novels and celebrity tell-alls with his publicly distributed letter, The History of My Calamities and public correspondence. In the context of the chapter, it suggests looking at the self or existence not just as a particular individual bound by time, but as part of a universal, timeless whole. Mr. Spitzer is reflecting on his own identity and existence, recognizing that he is more than the sum of his temporal experiences. The passage conveys his awareness of the fluidity and multiplicity of identity and existence, moving beyond the confines of linear time and fixed boundaries. The Latin phrase can be rendered in English as "from the perspective of the eternal". More loosely, it is commonly used to refer to an objective (or theoretically possible alternative) point of view. Spinoza's "eternal" perspective is reflected in his Ethics (Part V, Prop. XXIII, Scholium), where he applies Euclid's method (with the use of geometry) to philosophical inquiry, starting with God and nature, before moving to human emotions and the human intellect to reach an understanding of moral philosophy. By proceeding sub specie aeternitatis, Spinoza sought to arrive at an ethical theory that is as precise as Euclid's Elements. In the history of philosophy, this way of proceeding may be contrasted with Aristotle's. Aristotle's methodological differentiations in his "philosophy of human affairs" and his natural philosophy are grounded in the distinction between what is "better known to us" and things "better known in themselves", or what is "first for us" and what is "first by nature", a distinction that is deliberately discarded by Spinoza, and also by other modern philosophers.

This resonates with existentialist thought, which emphasizes the inherent incompleteness and absurdity of human life. The description of Mr. Spitzer "dreaming like the heart of God upon a world never created, uncreated, this world dreaming itself even when there was no counterpart" suggests a world that is in a constant state of becoming, and perhaps only exists within the mind of the dreamer. Mr. Spitzer's fear of being evicted from the "citadel" and being born into a world where he misses fundamental sensory experiences (smell of the rose, sound of birds) speaks to the existential anxiety of losing one's sense of self and belonging. The idea of a mother who is a "bearded man armored" challenges traditional notions of gender and identity. This can be linked to philosophical discussions about the social construction of gender and the fluidity of identity. The image of the "old jockey who dreamed that his dead horse lived" and the subsequent shock of realizing the dream's reality highlights the power of the unconscious and the irrational. This aligns with psychoanalytic theories, particularly those of Freud, which emphasize the influence of unconscious desires and repressed memories on human behavior. The phrase "We lived by an imperfect concatenation, even as we died—by echoes, tremblings, reverberations, sourceless thoughts" suggests that life is a series of disjointed and fragmented experiences. This aligns with Buddhist philosophy, which emphasizes the impermanence of all things and the illusory nature of the self.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer wonders if doubt should move mountains “which faith had not moved." This is a direct inversion of the common saying that faith can move mountains. This highlights a core philosophical tension between believing in something despite a lack of evidence (faith) and questioning everything (doubt). - Matthew 17:20. The image of the suffragette searching for a lost skirt, leading to the death of her lover, suggests the absurdity of human pursuits. The pursuit of something seemingly trivial (the skirt) leads to tragic consequences, mirroring the existentialist idea that life is inherently meaningless, and humans create their own meaning through their actions. The description of the skirt as "white lace gleaming through snow and its little flowers which were like the memories of little loves" blurs the lines between reality and memory. It suggests that our perceptions of reality are shaped by our past experiences and emotions, leading to a subjective and potentially distorted understanding of the world. The mention of the suffragette crying "Long live woman! Vive la femme! Viva la donna!" in many languages, "perhaps even in Sanskrit which was the language written upon a silent snowflake," touches on the philosophy of language. It suggests that language can be a powerful tool for expressing universal concepts (like the importance of women) but that there are also limits to what language can convey. There are "secret languages never to be translated into words," implying that some truths are beyond the reach of verbal expression. The reference to, "the suffragette who had lost her apostle" could also be referencing the loss of an ideal form. Platonism is the belief that everything we see is a shadow or "lesser" version of a perfect form. The loss of her apostle, who could be a student or follower, is also the loss of what the suffragette sees as a perfect version of herself. The next paragraph emphasizes the individual's choice and action in the face of an indifferent or absurd universe. The suffragette's decision to dress as a man can be seen as an assertion of her freedom and rejection of societal norms. The fantastical images of footmen and golden stairways highlight the human tendency to create meaning and beauty in a world that may ultimately be meaningless. The contrast between Cousin Hannah's practical clothing and the elaborate attire of other climbers could be interpreted as a reflection of the philosophical debate between idealism and materialism. The suffragette's focus on functionality suggests a more materialistic worldview, while the other climbers' emphasis on appearance could be seen as representing idealism. The repeated blurring of the lines between mountains and clouds, and the shifting perceptions of the moon, raise questions about the nature of reality and the limitations of human perception. The statement, "the moon had floated most amazingly distending worlds," suggests that reality is not fixed but is shaped by our individual perspectives. The image of the footman cutting a golden stairway from a frozen lake to the mountains of the moon could be an allusion to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. The stairway could represent the philosopher's ascent from the darkness of the cave (the material world) to the light of the sun (the realm of Forms). The mountains of the moon could symbolize a higher realm of knowledge and understanding. The paragraph's emphasis on nature, individual experience, and the search for spiritual meaning aligns with the themes of Transcendentalism. The suffragette's mountain climbing could be seen as a metaphor for the individual's journey to transcend the limitations of the material world and connect with a higher power or truth. The mention of "horizons unknown as the stars floated" could also be interpreted in a nihilistic way, suggesting that there are no ultimate goals or destinations and that all human endeavors are ultimately meaningless. At first it's a whimsical and imaginative description of mountain climbing, then, beneath the surface, it explores fundamental philosophical questions about freedom, reality, perception, and the meaning of life which invites the reader to think about their own philosophical reflections.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer, reflecting on the suffragette's life, wonders if "All might have been imaginary in this life as in this death." This relates to philosophical discussions about the nature of reality, perception, and the extent to which our experiences are shaped by our minds. The search through the suffragette's belongings is a search for truth and understanding, but the paragraph suggests that this search may be futile. "Surely her entire life could not have been a game of hide-and-seek, for although she was hiding—who was seeking for her?" This touches on the philosophical problem of epistemology, or how we can know what is true, and whether objective truth is even attainable. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the suffragette's death and its meaning. He wonders if death might be a "miracle," and questions whether she has found her love in death. This aligns with philosophical inquiries into the nature of death, the possibility of an afterlife, and the meaning of existence in the face of mortality. The paragraph suggests that time may not be linear or objective, but rather a subjective experience. "All might have been an indeterminate moment or one beyond this calendar of days, hours, years. And what calendar was ever kept in the long night?" This idea relates to philosophical discussions about the nature of time, its relationship to consciousness, and whether time is an objective reality or a human construct. The paragraph also presents love as a paradox, questioning whether it can ever be fully realized or understood. "There was the homeward music of the past and the music of the future which was never to be, and there was the music which could not be—and the music which was always to be..." This paradox is a recurring theme in philosophy, particularly in discussions about the nature of desire, attachment, and the limitations of human relationships. It is filled with dualities and opposing forces: life and death, reality and imagination, love and loss, male and female. This relates to philosophical concepts of duality, dialectics, and the idea that reality is composed of opposing forces that are constantly interacting. It questions the value of individual experience and the search for meaning. This aligns with philosophical discussions about existentialism, individualism, and the search for meaning in a seemingly absurd world.

Chapter 52

  • “Mr. Spitzer had trembled like a gambler for whom there would always be another shuffle” and the next paragraph. These two paragraphs use rich, poetic imagery and metaphor to explore themes of uncertainty, decay, memory, and intertwined fates. Mr. Spitzer is depicted as a liminal figure caught between reality and illusion, past and present, life and death, whose reflections on the suffragette reveal the elusive nature of truth and identity in the novel. The suffragette herself is a haunting presence (both fragile and magnetic, real and spectral) whose life and legacy resist simple comprehension, embodying the novel's complex interplay of reality and dream.The opening lines immediately establish a world governed by chance. Mr. Spitzer trembling "like a gambler" suggests a life where outcomes are unpredictable and determined by forces beyond individual control. This aligns with existentialist themes of the absurdity of existence and the lack of inherent meaning. The "faceless card" and "star of no known number" symbolize the limits of human knowledge. We can never fully grasp the forces shaping our lives, and there will always be elements of the unknown. This resonates with the existentialist emphasis on the limits of reason. The line "Yes, there was an external world, he knew now as it departed" is crucial. It indicates a loss of faith in an objective reality. The world is not fixed but is constantly slipping away, emphasizing the subjective experience. "He gave his belief when there was no reason for his belief" highlights a rejection of rationalism. Spitzer's faith is not based on evidence or logic but on something deeper, perhaps a Kierkegaardian "leap of faith" into the absurd. "For he reserved his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others. Their skepticism was his faith" is a complex statement. It suggests that Spitzer finds meaning in what others reject. This could be interpreted as a form of contrarianism, or as a deeper understanding that truth often lies in challenging conventional wisdom.

Chapter 52

  • The Swiss accusations against Cousin Hannah highlight the ethical problem of unintended consequences. Even if her actions were driven by noble intentions, such as seeking her lost love or advancing suffrage, they allegedly resulted in harm to others, such as causing snow-slides or burying trains. This relates to consequentialism, which evaluates actions based on their outcomes. There is a tension between progress and destruction. Cousin Hannah "uncovered some things" but "covered others," raising questions about whether progress inevitably involves loss or harm. This relates to dialectical thinking, where progress emerges from the conflict between opposing forces. The Swiss fear of Cousin Hannah potentially disrupting the stability of their nation reflects a conflict between individual freedom and the collective good. The Swiss are concerned about their community and way of life. This relates to political philosophy and the social contract. Mr. Spitzer questions the reliability of perception and the possibility of truly knowing anything. The mountains may be clouds, and the clouds may be mountains, highlighting the subjective nature of reality. This relates to skepticism and the questioning of empirical knowledge. The newspaper reports of the suffragette's adventures are presented as "blurred" and open to interpretation. This emphasizes the role of the observer in shaping reality and the difficulty of establishing objective truth. Mr. Spitzer's belief "when there was no reason for his belief" and his reservation of "his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others" suggests a rejection of conventional notions of truth based on empirical evidence or logical reasoning. This relates to philosophical movements like existentialism, which prioritize individual experience and meaning-making. The notion that Cousin Hannah's actions could cause "reverberations to eternity if not to infinity" implies a belief in the interconnectedness of all things and the far-reaching consequences of even seemingly small actions. This aligns with holistic philosophies that emphasize the unity of existence. The idea that "time and the dream were never married in her" suggests a rejection of linear time and an embrace of a more fluid, dreamlike reality. This relates to philosophies that challenge conventional notions of time, such as those found in process philosophy. Mr. Spitzer considers the possibility that Cousin Hannah might "ferry snow-crowned mountains of passage to another world" and "take all to that world where there was no mourning," suggesting a belief in transcendence or the possibility of escaping the limitations of earthly existence. These philosophical inferences are not presented as systematic arguments but rather as fragmented reflections that emerge from Mr. Spitzer's consciousness as he grapples with the legacy of Cousin Hannah.

Chapter 52

  • “Perhaps it was she who was the master of keys” grapples with the question of what happens after death. Mr. Spitzer contemplates whether the soul ("spirit") needs a physical exit, like a chimney, if the conventional routes ("doors and passage-ways") are closed. This reflects philosophical inquiries into the soul's immortality and its separation from the body. The idea that "death was unknown to those who loved, and death was unknown to those who loved not, and death was unknown to those who died" suggests that death remains an enigma regardless of one's experiences or beliefs. It's a state beyond comprehension, aligning with existentialist themes of the unknown and the limits of human knowledge. The paragraph questions whether our senses provide a complete picture of reality. The idea that "Even the closed door was not closed, for should death be better known than love? Not all the senses were ever sealed at once" suggests that there are realities beyond our immediate perception. The image of the butterfly escaping through the ear, "even when it was a door of the silence," implies that even in the absence of sound, there are avenues for experience or existence. The description of Mr. Spitzer as a night watchman in the "starry universe" raises questions about the nature of reality. Is he a real figure, or is he merely a figment of someone's imagination? His light awakening "other sleepers, those he never knew" suggests the interconnectedness of existence, even if we are unaware of it. The suggestion that he perhaps "had intended to lock and not to unlock" introduces the possibility that his actions may have unintended consequences, highlighting the limits of human control and the role of chance. The final lines emphasize Mr. Spitzer's role as the "only mourner among men," suggesting a profound sense of isolation and the burden of grief. His mourning for himself implies a recognition of his own mortality and the inevitability of loss. This connects to existentialist themes of individual responsibility and the search for meaning in a seemingly meaningless world.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer's meticulous accounting and listing is directly tied to his struggle with his identity, particularly his relationship with his deceased brother. He seeks a perfect balance, a mirrored reflection where everything in his life corresponds to his brother's, suggesting a desire to understand himself through this dualistic lens. The fear of "no differing counterpart" speaks to the existential anxiety of lacking a defined self, relying on another for definition. This resonates with philosophical concepts of identity formation, the "self" versus the "other," and the influence of external relationships on self-perception. Thinkers like Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir explored similar themes in existentialism. Spitzer's obsessive listing and indexing of even the most mundane objects (pearl buttons, rusted nail heads, etc.) reflects a deep-seated need to impose order on a chaotic world. He's trying to find patterns, connections, and a "common denominator" to make sense of existence. This aligns with the philosophical pursuit of metaphysics: trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality. The futility of Spitzer's efforts mirrors the inherent difficulties in finding absolute order or meaning in a world often perceived as absurd or chaotic (a key theme in existentialism and absurdism). The questions about the sail ("Was the sail unwinding the same as the winding sail?") touch on the philosophical problem of identity over time. Does something remain the same if its state changes? This is further complicated by the cyclical nature of the tides and the wagon wheels, implying a sense of eternal return or repetition. This connects to Heraclitus's famous saying, "No man ever steps in the same river twice," emphasizing the constant flux and change in the universe. The paragraph also hints at Nietzsche's concept of eternal recurrence. Spitzer's attempts to capture reality through lists and measurements are ultimately limited. His fear that "all the weight, as he had often complained, was on this weightless star" alludes to the disparity between the tangible and intangible, the concrete and abstract. He can list the physical properties of objects, but he cannot capture their essence or meaning. This is related to epistemology, the study of knowledge and its limitations. The paragraph suggests the impossibility of fully knowing or representing reality, as there will always be something missing or lost in translation. The description of Spitzer's actions creating "division as in division there was creation," suggests that in every act of creation, there is also an act of destruction. This mirrors the belief that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. This is connected to the concept of the "Tao" which states that everything is composed of two opposites, and that without the other, it cannot exist.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer's search through the house and trunks represents a quest for knowledge and understanding of the suffragette's life. The fact that he searches for "he knew not what" suggests that the nature of knowledge itself is uncertain. The "magnetic doors" that open on their own imply that some knowledge is revealed passively, not through active seeking. The idea that there were many differences between the suffragette's last sleep and her first sleep suggests a changing reality, shaped by experience and time. The "tumultuous life" alters the nature of her being. The reference to a "windowless seraglio or cave or darkened tower" relates to the mind as a prison or a space of limited perception. The idea of the "supernumerary love, a wife unknown" introduces the concept of hidden aspects of the self or unconscious desires. The paragraph delves into the nature of love and its mysteries. The "blind god of love" refers to the idea that love is irrational and indiscriminate. The image of the "turban-winder winding fields of consciousness" suggests that love can lead to a loss of individual identity and a merging of consciousnesses. The phrase "in the unwinding there should be no memory and no woman and no man" implies a fading of individual existence and a potential descent into nothingness. This reflects themes of nihilism and existentialism where existence is seen as meaningless and absurd. The individual's fading suggests a loss of self and meaning.

Chapter 68

  • "there was only one definition of reality, that it was real" emphasizes a tautological but deeply existential assertion: reality is defined by its own existence as experienced or known, regardless of its form. "even the unreal things were real," points to an inclusive, perhaps subjective or phenomenological, understanding of reality where things dismissed or marginalized by society (ignored, rejected, unloved) are nonetheless part of the fabric of reality. This echoes themes of illusion versus reality, and the permeability between them, which run throughout the novel. Philosophically, this passage represents a theme often associated with existentialism and phenomenology: that reality is defined by experience and perception rather than by fixed, external definitions. It also touches on the fluidity of reality, blurring lines between dream and waking life, appearance and essence, presence and absence. The passage conveys that reality is not limited to the tangible or socially accepted but includes dreams, illusions, forgotten or rejected beings, and all forms of existence or perception. It challenges rigid dichotomies and invites a broader, more inclusive understanding of what is real.

Chapter 70

  • "There is no return but the return of what is different, I suppose, and that by establishing relationships where none exist, we merely deceive ourselves into believing that life as a whole has a hidden, constant meaning like the unheard music of the spheres." The passage reflects a philosophical meditation on the unavoidability of change, the human compulsion to find or impose meaning, and the possibility that such meaning is not inherent but constructed. It challenges the belief in a fixed cosmic order and suggests that what we perceive as meaningful patterns may be self-deceptions, resonating with existentialist skepticism and the impermanence stressed in ancient and modern philosophies.

Plutarch functions as a symbol of the mother’s intellectual and cultural anchoring amidst her drifting consciousness, representing a link to enduring human wisdom and the complexities of love, fate, and history that permeate her visionary world.

Chapter 6

  • “You think that beauty is as beauty does”: The proverb says a person’s true beauty is in their character and actions, not their physical appearance. The older proverb is “handsome is as handsome does” (1500s). The sentiment is found in the writings of Geoffrey Chaucer in “The Wife of Bath’s Tale” (c. 1387) from The Canterbury Tales. Chaucer’s lines suggest that the most virtuous person, regardless of physical appearance, is the most beautiful. The Greek philosophers Plato and Aristotle linked beauty to virtue, order, and symmetry. This perspective influenced the development of the proverb, suggesting that inner qualities are just as important as outward appearance in determining beauty.
  • “the angels do not marry, for they are male and female in one body”: In Plato’s Symposium Aristophanes tells of the first humans, double beings later split in two, each half forever seeking the other.

  • “that dream within the dream”: This may refer to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “A Dream within a Dream” (1849), which says, “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream.” This dream within a dream is a recurring theme throughout the book. The idea that life is a dream goes back to Plato, Aristotle, and Descartes. The first stanza ends with that statement, and the last stanza turns it into a question: “Is all that we see or seem / But a dream within a dream?” This symbolizes the recursive, elusive quality of existence in the novel: a reality constantly refracted through multiple dreamlike states that challenge the notion of a fixed, singular truth.
